about: Seed knowledge converted from immersive-episteme (six traditions plus shared craft science) and inferential-system (block printing, terracotta, wood carving draft graphs). Claims carry their quoted passages and sources. 'PROVISIONAL' means a verbatim quote was re-found by the upstream source check; 'HYPOTHESIS' means no checked quote (inferential drafts, or a source that states it as a hypothesis). Imports are written by the system actor 'import' and are never above PROVISIONAL.

traditions.name: Ajrakh resist block printing (Kutch Ajrakh)
traditions.summary: Ajrakh is a resist- and mordant-dyed, hand block-printed cotton textile made by Khatri printers whose ancestors came from Sindh; in India it is centred at Ajrakhpur, Dhamadka and Khavda in Kutch, with related practice in Barmer. Its 14-16 stage sequence combines lime-gum and mud resists, iron-black and alum mordant printing, indigo vat dyeing and madder or alizarin red dyeing, traditionally in a four-colour palette and often printed identically on both sides. After the 2001 earthquake and deteriorating water at Dhamadka, printers founded Ajrakhpur; the craft was registered as the 'Kutch Ajrakh' GI (application 1050) in 2024.

region.place: Ajrakhpur (also Dhamadka and Khavda); related practice in Barmer (Rajasthan) and Sindh (Pakistan)

traditions.name: Bagh print (hand block printing of Bagh, Madhya Pradesh)
traditions.summary: Bagh print is a hand block printing tradition of Bagh town in Dhar district, Madhya Pradesh, practised mainly by the Khatri (chhipa) community, and registered as a Geographical Indication. Its signature is geometric and floral repeat patterns printed in red and black on a white ground with mordants (alum for red, iron for black) that develop colour when the cloth is boiled with alizarin and dhavda flowers in a copper vat (bhatti). The process depends heavily on flowing river water for repeated washing.

traditions.name: Bagru hand block printing
traditions.summary: Bagru hand block printing is a registered Geographical Indication (2011) of Bagru and three neighbouring villages in Jaipur district, Rajasthan, practised by the hereditary Chhipa printer community using carved wooden blocks. Its classic Syahi-Begar style prints an iron 'syahi' (black) and alum 'begar' (red) mordant on harda-treated, off-white cotton and develops both colours in one alizarin/madder dyebath; its Dabu style uses a black-clay resist paste followed by indigo and yellow dyeing.

traditions.name: Dabu mud-resist block printing
traditions.summary: Dabu is a Rajasthani hand-block technique in which a paste of mud, lime and natural gum is block-printed onto cloth, dusted with sawdust and sun-dried so that it resists a cold indigo bath; resist-and-dye cycles are repeated to build layered shades. Akola village in Chittorgarh district, home to Chhipa printers on the Beduch river, is widely described as its centre of origin. Recipes vary between centres, and in present-day Akola tar-based resists have partly displaced mud.

traditions.name: Machilipatnam (Pedana) block-printed Kalamkari
traditions.summary: Machilipatnam Kalamkari is a hand-block-printed cotton textile tradition from Pedana and neighbouring villages near Machilipatnam (Krishna district, Andhra Pradesh), registered as a Geographical Indication (application no. 90; certificate 2008). Cloth is bleached, treated with myrobalan, block-printed with iron (kasim) and alum (karam) mordants, boiled in alizarin with plant additives, overprinted with yellow and indigo, and fixed through repeated washing in flowing water and sun-drying. The tradition descends from the Golconda-era port trade in Masulipatnam painted and printed cottons for Persia and Europe, where blocks progressively replaced the hand-drawn kalam.

traditions.name: Sanganeri hand block printing
traditions.summary: Sanganeri hand block printing is a hand block-printed textile tradition of Sanganer town, about 16 km from Jaipur, registered as a Geographical Indication (application no. 147) by the Calico Printers Co-operative Society. It is known for fine, repetitive floral butis and butas on a white ground, printed by Chhipa printers with blocks carved by Kharadi block-makers, traditionally using a harda (myrobalan) pre-treatment, iron (syahi) and alum (begar) mordants dyed in alizarin/madder, sun-bleaching, dabu mud-resist and indigo. Since the 1960s the craft has faced competition from screen printing and a large shift to synthetic dyes, and the cluster is associated with documented water pollution.

traditions.name: Shared craft science
traditions.summary: Shared scientific mechanisms and materials of Indian hand-block printing: metal-mordant complexation of anthraquinone reds, iron-tannin blacks and their fibre damage, indigo vat reduction and re-oxidation, physical resists, tannin pre-treatment, cloth preparation, sun bleaching and print-paste rheology. Mechanisms are stated only as far as the cited literature supports. Several rest on studies of other systems (Turkey red, paper, modern screen printing, pure clay films) and are flagged as analogies.

sources.notes: Detailed cluster documentation of Akola: location (Bhopalsagar tehsil, Chittorgarh), ~200 practitioners, allied communities, 14 traditional block designs, current tar/oil/rogan resist replacing mud (mud cracked), naphthol + red salt reds, ash dusting, indigo cold bath green->blue, boiling to remove tar, tools, challenges (fumes, water use, groundwater pollution). Intro inconsistently names Udaipur district. Fact-check 2026-10-14: page also explains naphthol/diazo salt coupling and records the zigzag phetiya border and kadhai-like boilers.

sources.title: Craft Name: Dabu (Craft Katha)
authors: All India Artisans and Craftworkers Welfare Association (AIACA)
sources.notes: Black clay, lime and natural gum; "fermented mud paste"; light crackle effect; 5-15 days and 2-4 artisans per piece; attributes craft to Khatri community; claims GI tag in 2023 (contradicted by S5). Fact-check: page says "Khatris" and lists "Light crackle effect visible in resist areas" as an authenticity marker; no publication date (footer 2025).

sources.title: Dabu Block Printing
sources.notes: Dabu described as "a cold-water resist" and a "mud-resist" using fine desert sand of Rajasthan, used during an indigo bath; reports certain patterns printed only on certain weaves of set width and length depending on the communities. Judged 2026-11-08 (DR-134) on its archived copy: kept: Maiwa, a natural-dye house working with Rajasthani block printers for 40 years, describes dabu as a cold-water mud resist used in the indigo bath and its community-specific patterns, matching the tradition. Archived copy: D:/Work/IIT-KGP/Paper_1-artifacts/sources/dabu-2026-11-07/S21.html.

sources.title: 'Bagru' - A Traditional Printing Technique of Rajasthan
sources.notes: Added by fact-check. Bagru-centred (not Akola). Scouring with a paste of cow dung, soda ash and sesame oil ("Hari sarana"); harda (myrobalan) wash whose tannic acid acts as mordant for the iron of the black (syahi); dabu = lime, "Bedhan" (worm-spoiled wheat flour) and black clay, mashed, left overnight, strained; Kaligar/Dolidar/Gawarbali dabu types; sawdust; indigo then pomegranate, then alum-water rinse to fix colour, alum quantity varying with dabu strength. Year from PDF metadata (2012); no peer review.

sources.title: Indian Block-Printed Textiles: Past and Present
sources.notes: Added by fact-check. Museum conservator essay (15 Nov 2016) with fieldwork at Bagru, Akola, Ajrakhpur, Sri Kalahasti: Dabu is "the most common resist used for indigo today", often showing crack lines where dye penetrated cracks in the resist; photo of an indigo vat at Akola (2015). Dung scouring and harde/alum/iron passages refer to Ajrakh/general practice, not Dabu.

sources.title: Block printing the impermeable clay Dabu
sources.publisher: Craft Revival Trust Archive via Google Arts & Culture
sources.notes: Documented at Deesa, Gujarat (not Akola). Paste of river-bed silt, local gum, lime, sugarcane molasses and water; kneaded by stamping over several days; strained; sawdust over wet paste; sun-dried until hard; dip-dyed; repeated per colour.

sources.title: Drying the dabu clay paste
sources.publisher: Craft Revival Trust Archive via Google Arts & Culture
sources.notes: Documented at Bagru. Wet dabu dusted with beden (insect-eaten wheat-flour waste) to dry quickly and prevent smudging; dabu printing often done by women at home or in karkhanas.

sources.title: GI Application No. 845 - Aakola Dabu Prints
sources.notes: Applicant Udhyam Protsahan Sansthan; filed 04-03-2022; Class 24 handicrafts; status Pre Examination (not registered) as of access date. Statement of Case listed but not read.

sources.title: Hand Block Printing of Akola, Rajasthan
sources.publisher: Global InCH - International Journal of Living Heritage
sources.notes: Akola dabu types phetia and nangna; three resists of increasing strength: chuna/lime (kirana), mitti/mud, rait/sand; also describes a boiled bedja-gum + oil hot resist with ash dusting, metal blocks, naphthol/alizarin. Places Akola in Udaipur district. Fact-check: Phetia worn by Jat and Chaudhury women after childbirth or at weddings; nangna by Gujjar women (occasion not given).

sources.title: Dabu/Hand Block Printing of Rajasthan
sources.publisher: Global InCH - International Journal of Living Heritage
sources.notes: Bagru-centred: fabric washed and sun-dried, paste of gum, mud and waste wheat chaff, printed on large tables, sun-dried, dyed, washed.

sources.title: Dabu Print of Gujarat
sources.publisher: Global InCH - International Journal of Living Heritage
sources.notes: Dabu in Deesa, Ahmedabad, Jamnagar; paste of mud and local baval gum; washing at each new colour.

sources.title: Bed curtain, Coromandel Coast, c.1700 (IS.121-1950)
sources.notes: Coromandel chintz technique: alum mordant for red, iron mordant for black; indigo needs no mordant so wax resist used; green = yellow over indigo.

authors: Reddy, Renuka (guest post; posted by Avalon Fotheringham)
sources.notes: Practitioner account (not Pedana-specific): buffalo milk fat said to prevent dye spreading; uncertainty chay vs madder roots in trade; washing/cow-dung bleaching between colours. Fact-check: Reddy visited Machilipatnam and Srikalahasti; dated 6 Oct 2015.

sources.title: Kalamkari: An Introduction
sources.notes: Machilipatnam vs Srikalahasti: karkhanas, block makers from carpenter community, teak blocks one per colour, washing at Kalia Canal, iron boiling vessels, gaja leaves; states alum is NOT used for red at Machilipatnam (conflicts with S3/S4). sources.title: Kalamkari Woodblock Makers (interview)

sources.title: As fake Kalamkari takes over the market, the original struggles in Andhra's Pedana
sources.notes: Journalism with artisan testimony: cow-dung soak and pond washing, myrobalan + buffalo milk, copper-vessel boiling, black from iron scrap/jaggery/salt in buried jar 21 days, starch/alum/soap finish; screen-printing competition and canal pollution; states GI 2012. Fact-check: dated 24 Jul 2018; article step order matches Craftmark (scour, myrobalan, print, wash, boil, wash, starch, second colour, alum, soap).

sources.notes: Purchased from the Great Exhibition 1851; Sanganer served the Jaipur court; blocks usually teak, most esteemed from Pethapur; indigo and madder, green from indigo plus a yellow (probably turmeric); offset rows of florals with Mughal 17th-c. origins. sources.title: Syahi Begar | Sanganer Print
sources.notes: Craft-documentation organisation: syahi (scrap iron, horseshoes, gur), begar (alum, tree gum, geru), harda pila-karna, teluni scouring, copper tamda on bhatti, dhaura ka phool, river washing and sun drying; migration story; chemical dyes from 1980s; social categories of designs. Fact-check: kind changed from practitioner_testimony to researcher_interpretation; this is an unsigned narrative article by a craft-documentation/retail organisation, not a first-hand practitioner account.

sources.title: Sanganeri
authors: Impart Encyclopedia of Art (formerly MAP Academy)
sources.publisher: Art & Photography Foundation (Museum of Art & Photography, Bengaluru)
sources.notes: Encyclopedia entry: migration from Kathiawar after Mughal-Maratha campaigns; Chhipa; Sawai Jai Singh patronage conjectured; river Dhoondh; bhant motifs (400+ types); syahi begar / court / temple design categories; Mughal and East India Company influence on motifs; block carvers, Farrukhabad migration 1970s; GI 2010.

sources.title: Fiber-Safe Extraction of Red Mordant Dyes from Hair Fibers
sources.publisher: Journal of the American Institute for Conservation 34(3):195-206
sources.notes: Peer-reviewed conservation chemistry. Mordants as metal salts forming insoluble dye complexes; figure of a Ca-Al alizarin lake adapted from Kiel & Heertjes; alizarin forms six-member chelate rings with Al; acid extraction 'probably' works by replacing the metal ion with H+; large complexes likely physically trapped. Study is on hair (protein) fibres; mechanism statements are general.

sources.title: Indian Block-Printed Textiles: Past and Present
sources.notes: Met Perspectives article dated 15 Nov 2016 (author role not stated on page). Cleaning with camel dung, castor oil, soda ash, sun bleaching 'by oxidation'; myrobalan (harde) as mordant precursor; alum paste fixes red only where printed; on the 13th-14th c. Met fragment the darker purple was printed with iron acetate from fermented scrap iron which with myrobalan caused fibre loss; Dabu mud resist with crack lines; indigo oxidises on air exposure; Indian red dye plants (Al, munjeet, chay); synthetic alizarin and indigo common today.

sources.title: Chintz (process sample), museum no. T.1-1920
sources.notes: Coromandel Coast process: alum and iron mordants applied by kalam; chay-root bath gives red on alum and black on iron; wax resist for indigo; cloth washed and bleached between colours. Year is acquisition (made c.1919).

sources.title: Charting Chintz: Making the Fabric
sources.notes: Experimental reconstruction (Beaulieu manuscript): scouring, myrobalan and milk soaks, alum (red) and iron-water (black) outlines, madder bath under 60 C, repeated dunging and sun bleaching (sun lamps substituted). Year approximate (page shows 2020-2026 copyright).

sources.title: Dyeing cotton fabrics is an ancient Indian art
sources.notes: Science journalism (published 15 Dec 1992). For madder, cloth first dipped in tannic solution then mordanted; alum gives red, iron acetate black; in contemporary Masulipatnam iron acetate replaced indigo for large black areas despite its known corrosive qualities; indigo reduced by fermentation to soluble indigo white and fixed by air oxidation; resists of gum and mud or wax.

sources.title: Block printing the impermeable clay Dabu
sources.publisher: Google Arts & Culture (Craft Revival Trust archive)
sources.notes: Archive caption (Craft Revival Trust, 2009, Deesa, Gujarat): Dabu paste of dried river-bed silt, local natural gum, lime, sugar-cane molasses and water, kneaded several days and strained; sawdust sprinkled; sun-dried till hard; dip-dyed; repeated per colour. Documentation of one workshop, not chemical analysis.

sources.title: Effects of Aqueous Light Bleaching on the Subsequent Aging of Paper
sources.publisher: Journal of the American Institute for Conservation 31(3):289-311
sources.notes: Peer-reviewed conservation science on light bleaching of wet (immersed) paper, by sunlight or lamps. Mechanism statement: a chromophore absorbs light and is converted to a reactive peroxide or free radical, which causes (usually oxidative) change; chromophores become colourless products; light can also degrade paper components. Paper, not cotton cloth: analogue only for Indian sun bleaching.

sources.title: Production and validation of model iron-tannate dyed textiles for use as historic textile substitutes in stabilisation treatment studies
sources.notes: Peer-reviewed, with undyed controls. Fe(II) + hydrolysable tannins form blue-black iron(III)-tannate, colour from Fe(III)-O charge transfer; cellulose can bind tannic acid (H-bonding) and metal ions; dyed textiles surface pH 2.65-3.91 vs 5.36-7.46 undyed; dyed cotton lost tensile strength faster and more than undyed during accelerated ageing (80 C, 58% RH), attributed to acid hydrolysis and metal-catalysed oxidation. Model dyes from iron salt + tannic acid, not Indian iron acetate/myrobalan.

sources.title: Topology of desiccation crack patterns in clay and invariance of crack interface area with thickness
sources.publisher: arXiv:1412.2842 (preprint); published in The European Physical Journal E (2015), doi:10.1140/epje/i2015-15083-6
sources.notes: Fetched the arXiv preprint (published version not read). Drying clay (bentonite) slurry films on glass: below a critical cracking thickness films dry without cracking; crack spacing is of the order of film thickness; thicker layers give fewer, wider cracks; composition, drying rate, humidity, substrate affect patterns. Pure clay on glass, not Dabu on cloth: physical analogue only.

sources.title: Turkey red dyeing in late-19th century Glasgow: Interpreting the historical process through re-creation and chemical analysis for heritage research and conservation (PhD thesis)
sources.notes: Alum = potassium aluminium sulfate; aluminium acetate ('red liquor') considered better for cellulose; red colour is a lake of alizarin, aluminium and calcium; 27Al ssNMR shows six-fold coordinated Al on oiled-and-alumed calico and replica Turkey red; tannins chelate metals and 'probably' attract more aluminium. Context is European Turkey red (oil-mordant process), not Indian block printing.

sources.title: Experimental Treatment for Black-dyed Cotton Textiles Using Japanese Adhesives Funori and Nikawa
sources.publisher: Science for Conservation (Hozon Kagaku) No. 63, Tokyo National Research Institute for Cultural Properties
sources.notes: Lab study (ferrous sulfate + tannic acid on cotton). Introduction (citing earlier literature): iron + tannins give blacks/greys/browns; acidic process causing hydrolytic degradation of cellulose; iron-catalysed decomposition makes fibre weak and brittle; analogous to iron-gall-ink corrosion. Own measurement: extract pH of unaged dyed control 4.08 vs 6.85 undyed; pH falls and fragility rises with accelerated ageing. No aged undyed tensile control, so the strength loss is not isolated to iron in this study.

sources.title: Microbial Communities Associated With Indigo Fermentation That Thrive in Anaerobic Alkaline Environments
sources.notes: Indigo insoluble, leucoindigo soluble; reduction by indigo-reducing bacteria or sodium dithionite; brief air exposure oxidises leucoindigo; traditional vats kept at pH > 10.3-10.5 with lime hydrate; anaerobic alkaline conditions. Japanese sukumo vats.

sources.title: Influence of Cotton Pre-Treatment on Dyeing with Onion and Pomegranate Peel Extracts
sources.notes: Cotton impurities (pectin, proteins, organic acids, waxes, fats) give hydrophobicity; scouring removes them; most natural dyes have affinity for protein rather than cellulose fibres; mordants key for fastness; iron salts gave the most achromatic shades; pomegranate peel (28% tannins) is a tannin dye and the authors attribute part of its behaviour to tannin acting as a mordant (interpretation, not measured).

sources.title: Enzymatic desizing of cotton: a review
sources.publisher: International Journal of Management, IT and Engineering 4(1)
sources.notes: Warp threads coated with sizing agent (mostly starch) to prevent breakage; size must be removed before dyeing; amylase desizing. Review in a lower-tier journal; industrial context.

sources.title: The influence of mixed thickeners on printing over lyocell knitted fabric
sources.notes: Print sharpness, penetration and colour yield depend on paste viscosity and rheology; viscosity depends on the thickener; low-viscosity paste spreads and penetrates deeply; pseudoplastic paste has lower viscosity as shear rate increases; guar gum (galactomannan) pastes above 0.5% are pseudoplastic. Modern reactive-dye screen printing on lyocell: used here only as an analogue for block-printing pastes.

sources.title: Bleaching cotton in textile conservation: a closer look using atomic force microscopy
sources.notes: Photochemical and chemical attack can yellow cotton; discolouration lessened by oxidative or reductive bleaching; bleaching generally accepted to impart damage. Does not study sunlight bleaching itself.

sources.title: Comprehensive Review on Fruit of Terminalia chebula: Traditional Uses, Phytochemistry, Pharmacology, Toxicity, and Pharmacokinetics
sources.notes: Fruit tannins predominantly hydrolysable (gallotannins, ellagitannins, chebulic ellagitannins incl. chebulagic/chebulinic acid); 60 tannin compounds reported; during sunlight-drying of the fruit these degrade to gallic, ellagic and chebulic acids. No dyeing content.

concepts.name: Kutch Ajrakh (Ajrakh resist block printing)
concepts.description: Kutch Ajrakh is an elaborate resist block-printing technique involving a series of direct and resist printing and dyeing steps.

concepts.name: Sindh and Indus-region origins
concepts.description: Ajrakh printing originally came from Sindh.

concepts.name: Khatri migration from Sindh to Kutch
concepts.description: The technique came to Kutch from Sindh some 400 years ago at the behest of the King of Kutch, who invited Khatri craftsmen to the banks of the Dhamadka river.

concepts.name: Dhamadka as the historic centre
concepts.description: Ajrakh activities prevailed at Dhamadka for the past 450 years because of a water source from a stream of the Indus river; this stream dried up in 1989.

concepts.name: 2001 earthquake and founding of Ajrakhpur
concepts.description: After a massive earthquake in 2001 the block printers were forced to relocate and settled in Ajrakhpur; over 100 families live there with 30 official workshops.

concepts.name: Maldhari pastoralist clientele and traditional use
concepts.description: The fabric was traditionally worn by members of the royal court and the pastoral Maldhari community; men used it as cummerbunds, lungis, turbans and shoulder cloths.

concepts.name: Shift to synthetic dyes and natural-dye revival
concepts.description: Alizarin, invented in 1868, rapidly superseded madder; madder use almost disappeared and is now seeing a revival.

concepts.name: Partition and the Sindh-Kutch connection
concepts.description: Before Partition ajrakh was worn by Sindhi Muslim animal-keepers in Sindh, Kutch and Marwar.

concepts.name: Fustat trade fragments
concepts.description: 15th-century resist-printed fragments from Gujarat were found at Fustat in Egypt.

concepts.name: Ajrakh in Barmer, Rajasthan
concepts.description: Ajrakh printing is practised at Kachchh and Barmer.

concepts.name: GI registration of Kutch Ajrakh
concepts.description: Application 1050 for Kutch Ajrakh was made by Ajarakhpur Hastkala Vikas Sangathan, facilitated by the Textiles Committee, Ministry of Textiles.

concepts.name: Iron content of process water
concepts.description: Presence of iron in the water supply dulls and darkens the final result; alum, tin or chrome deposits help brighten colours.

concepts.name: Water availability and falling water tables
concepts.description: Ajrakh is described as a 16-stage, water-intensive technique; an artisan states that the craftsmen's requirement is to recycle about 1 lakh litres of water every day.

concepts.name: Soft water as a siting factor
concepts.description: Ajrakh printing got concentrated where extra soft water was available.

concepts.name: Sun, heat and time of day
concepts.description: Khariyanu outline printing is usually preferred in the morning; kut printing in the afternoon; gach printing later in the day so the cloth is dry and resist does not spread.

concepts.name: Monsoon humidity
concepts.description: Monsoon humidity slows production.

concepts.name: Cotton (and silk) base cloth
concepts.description: Artisans procure cotton fabric from 60s to 120s count depending on end use; silk Ajrakh is made for customised needs.

concepts.name: Neerani (castor oil, soda ash and camel dung emulsion)
concepts.description: Neerani is a thoroughly emulsified mixture of castor oil, soda ash and camel dung; soda ash was historically obtained from the ash of a local desert plant.

concepts.name: Harde (myrobalan, Terminalia chebula)
concepts.description: Harde is a yellow astringent paste from dried powdered Terminalia chebula fruits containing high levels of tannic acid.

concepts.name: Khariyanu resist paste (lime and tree gum)
concepts.description: Kiriyana resist paste consists of babool gum and lime diluted in water.

concepts.name: Kut (iron-water black paste)
concepts.description: Kut is made from jaggery or molasses in which scrap iron such as horseshoes and gram flour have been fermented for ten to fifteen days; the iron-water is mixed with tree gum.

concepts.name: Alum (fatakdi)
concepts.description: Alum is used as a mordant to fasten the colours.

concepts.name: Tamarind seed paste (pa)
concepts.description: Alum is suspended in a sticky paste of boiled powder from roasted and ground tamarind seeds (kachika).

concepts.name: Gach mud resist (clay, millet flour, gum)
concepts.description: Gach is a smooth paste of tree gum, clay (lal mitti), water and millet flour; alum is added to half of it.

concepts.name: Dusting agents (sawdust, cow dung, rice husk)
concepts.description: Sawdust or finely powdered cow dung is sprinkled immediately after printing the gach pastes to prevent the wet clay from smudging.

concepts.name: Indigo (natural Indigofera tinctoria or synthetic)
concepts.description: Indigo can be natural (Indigofera tinctoria) or synthetic 'German' indigo; natural indigo is fermented with lime, dates and soda; synthetic indigo often has 'Hydros' added.

concepts.name: Indian madder (majith/majeeta, Rubia cordifolia)
concepts.description: Indian madder roots (Rubia cordifolia), locally majeeta, link to the alum mordant on cotton to develop red where pa and gach were printed.

concepts.name: Synthetic alizarin
concepts.description: Alizarin, first synthesised in 1868 by Graebe and Liebermann, superseded madder and also requires alum to attach colour.

concepts.name: Dhawri flowers (dhaori na phool)
concepts.description: Cloth is boiled in a solution of tamarix (dhawri) with madder, al or alizarin.

concepts.name: Secondary yellow/green dye sources
concepts.description: Yellow from pomegranate (dadam), turmeric (haldi), flame of the forest and marigold; green from indigo with pomegranate or turmeric.

concepts.name: Camel dung (tapano solution)
concepts.description: Dyed cloth is soaked in a camel-dung solution and spread on river sand in the sun for tapano.

concepts.name: Hand-carved wooden printing blocks
concepts.description: Blocks in the first printing stage are of shisham and those in the third and fourth stages of teak; blocks are soaked in mustard oil when not in use.

concepts.name: Tari (printing tray)
concepts.description: The tari is made of wood with two handles and layered with chhapri, kantan (jute cloth), foam and fine cotton; foam and fine cloth are removed for less fine printing.

concepts.name: Dhoki (washing paddle)
concepts.description: A paddle called dhoki, made from babool wood, is used to help dislodge emulsified oils during washing.

concepts.name: Underground indigo vat (kun)
concepts.description: Natural indigo is fermented in an underground vat; a vat need only be made once and can be kept active, sometimes for decades.

concepts.name: Copper dye pot and stirring sticks
concepts.description: Alizarin or madder is heated in a large copper pot over a low fire, and cloth is continuously stirred using two sticks.

concepts.name: Washing tanks / river washing
concepts.description: Washing and beating at the washing tanks removes resist paste, loose indigo and tamarind paste.

concepts.name: Saaj (scouring and softening)
concepts.description: Pre-treatment involves a minimum of three soakings in neerani; the procedure is repeated eight to ten times until suitable saponification is achieved.

concepts.name: Washing and beating
concepts.description: Clean water is used to work the soap through the cloth; washing is a rigorous cycle of soaking and beating until all foam is wrung out.

concepts.name: Kasano (harde pre-mordanting)
concepts.description: The cloth is soaked in harde and dried in the sun without rinsing; tannin is an essential pre-mordant aiding adhesion of printed mordants.

concepts.name: Khariyanu (lime-gum resist outline printing)
concepts.description: Outlines where white is required are printed with a carved block and a lime and tree-gum resist paste.

concepts.name: Kut (iron-black printing)
concepts.description: Areas where black is required are printed with kut paste, usually an infill (datla) between khariyanu outlines.

concepts.name: Pa (alum mordant printing for red)
concepts.description: Pa, a smooth paste of alum in tamarind-seed paste, is printed with blocks patterned for the mavi areas where red is required.

concepts.name: Gach (alum-bearing mud resist)
concepts.description: Gach with alum is printed where larger red areas are required (red ground gudh or mavi infill); the clay and millet resist indigo while the alum acts as mordant.

concepts.name: Dhori gach (plain mud resist) and dusting
concepts.description: Dhori gach, without alum, is printed over previously printed white, black and pa-red areas that did not receive gach; sawdust or powdered cow dung is sprinkled immediately after.

stage.title: Dhori gach (plain mud resist) and dusting

concepts.name: Indigo dyeing (kun me burana)
concepts.description: The first stage of dyeing is called 'kun me burana'; the fabric is folded (fara) and dipped in the indigo vat.

concepts.name: Washing out resists
concepts.description: Washing begins gently to loosen clay without smudging, then becomes vigorous soaking and beating; remaining on the fibres are indigo, kut black, alum mordants and resisted whites.

concepts.name: Red dyeing (rang) with madder or alizarin
concepts.description: Alizarin crystals or steeped madder roots are heated in a copper pot; dyeing the purest reds continues for up to four hours.

stage.title: Red dyeing (rang) with madder or alizarin

concepts.name: Tapano (dung soak and sun-bleaching of whites)
concepts.description: Madder often leaves a pinkish tinge on whites; the cloth is soaked in camel dung, spread on sandy river banks in the sun and sprinkled with water over at least three days.

stage.title: Tapano (dung soak and sun-bleaching of whites)

concepts.name: Vichharana (final wash)
concepts.description: The final washing and beating removes loose colour; it is usually done early in the morning when water is cool.

concepts.name: Finishing (pressing and packaging)
concepts.description: Once washed completely, artisans do ancillary activities like pressing and packaging.

concepts.name: Judging saaj completion by lather and feel
concepts.description: Saaj can take many days depending on the level of impurities; by the third or fourth steeping a rich lather leaves the cloth bright white and soft.

concepts.name: Adjusting paste consistency to line fineness
concepts.description: Gum is soaked and sieved many times to make the paste smooth; for finer outlines the paste must be thicker.

concepts.name: Keeping lime and alum apart
concepts.description: Khariyanu paste must not spread onto areas where red is required, or the lime will discharge subsequent alum.

concepts.name: Scheduling stages by time of day
concepts.description: Morning is preferred for khariyanu; kut in the afternoon; guch later in the day so the cloth is dry; final wash early morning in cool water.

concepts.name: Choosing number of indigo dips and intermediate reprinting
concepts.description: If two shades of blue are required the cloth is reprinted between immersions; the darkest blues may need three or four immersions.

concepts.name: Watching the red dye bath
concepts.description: The fire is kept low and the cloth watched; if colour spreads into white areas, a handful of dried tamarisk flowers is added.

concepts.name: Tasting the indigo vat
concepts.description: Most Khatri printers could dip a finger in the vat, taste it and judge the shade and quality.

concepts.name: Registering double-sided prints
concepts.description: A printer must be very accurate so designs match on both sides; the fabric should be partly wet; corner registration marks help.

concepts.name: Choosing natural or synthetic dyes
concepts.description: Some printers serve both natural and chemical dye markets according to market demand.

concepts.name: Four-colour palette with cosmological reading
concepts.description: Red stands for Earth, black for darkness, white for clouds and blue for the universe itself.

concepts.name: Non-figurative geometric symmetry
concepts.description: An artisan quoted by Khamir describes Ajrakh as an Islamic design art with no figures, crafted with geometrical forms.

concepts.name: Both-sided (double-sided) printing
concepts.description: Historically Ajrakh has been printed on both sides so herders leaving before sunrise could wear it either way.

concepts.name: Border-and-field layout with named motifs
concepts.description: Both ends are decorated and three sides carry fixed border designs; only the central motif changes.

concepts.name: Designs as community identity markers
concepts.description: Maldhari groups (Nodai, Haleputra, Sama, Sumra, Jat) each had distinct styles and palettes that Khatris did not change.

concepts.name: Multi-block design sets
concepts.description: Each design is a set of four to six blocks.

concepts.name: Finished four-colour ajrakh cloth
concepts.description: Remaining on the fibres after washing are indigo blue, kut black, alum mordant and resisted white; red develops in red dyeing.

concepts.name: Traditional garments and textiles
concepts.description: Traditionally used as shoulder wrap, lungi, kammarband, chaddar and rajai by men; odhani and ghaghara by women.

concepts.name: Double-sided ajrakh as prestige cloth
concepts.description: Double-sided Ajrakh was the most expensive and only the rich could afford it.

concepts.name: Contemporary products and markets
concepts.description: Today ajrakh is made into bed sheets, saris, salwar-kameez material and stoles.

concepts.name: Saponification scouring in saaj
concepts.description: Grey cotton carries oils, pectin and wax that reduce absorbency and must be removed; neerani cycles are repeated until suitable saponification is achieved.

concepts.name: Lime blocking of alum and iron
concepts.description: The lime will discharge subsequent applications of alum.

concepts.name: Madder staining of whites and its clearing
concepts.description: Colour compounds in madder are more complex than synthetic alizarin, so madder often leaves a pinkish tinge on whites.

concepts.name: Warm wash water dissolving alum
concepts.description: Warm afternoon water may dissolve some of the alum.

concepts.name: Kutch, Barmer and Sindh ajrakh
concepts.description: The process and designs are common to Sindh, Kutch and Barmer.

concepts.name: When did Khatri printers settle in Kutch?
concepts.description: The GI journal gives about 400 years ago for the craft's arrival in Kutch from Sindh and for the Khatri settlement in Dhamadka, and 450 years of Ajrakh activity at Dhamadka.

concepts.name: Etymology of 'Ajrakh'
concepts.description: Ajrakh means 'keep it to-day' and also 'beautifying'.

concepts.name: Order and number of red and indigo stages
concepts.description: Sequence in the GI journal's Proof of Origin section: harda, alum print, red dye bath, mud resist, indigo.

concepts.name: Does natural-dyed ajrakh regulate temperature?
concepts.description: The GI text claims the fabric cools by day and warms by night due to indigo and natural dyes opening and closing its pores.

concepts.name: Cause and level of iron rise in Dhamadka water
concepts.description: Iron rose drastically after the earthquake.

concepts.name: Bagh print
concepts.description: Bagh prints are recognised by geometric repetitive patterns, mainly red and black block printed on a predominantly white base, using natural (vegetable) colours.

concepts.name: Bagh town and the Baghini river
concepts.description: Bagh is located at about 22°22'N 74°46'E with an average elevation of about 240 m; the main production centre is Bagh and the Kukshi area of Dhar district.

concepts.name: Khatri migration from Larkana, Sindh
concepts.description: The Khatri community of chhipas is believed to have come to Bagh about 400 years ago from Larkana in Sindh, famous for its Ajrak prints.

concepts.name: Ismail Khatri family route: Sindh, Pali, Gautampur, Manawar, Bagh (1962)
concepts.description: Ismail Khatri said his ancestors moved out of Sind, settled in Pali (near Jodhpur), moved to Gautampur in Malwa after a famine, and then to Manawar in Nimar.

concepts.name: Alternative origin accounts (Jawad / Rajasthan; ~1000 years)
concepts.description: Bagh hand block printing is believed to be about one thousand years old, passed down within families; the exact date of origin is difficult to point out.

concepts.name: Prints for specific communities and Adivasi wear
concepts.description: Artisans formerly made different prints and even different clothes for different communities and castes (e.g. Brahmin, Khatri, Harijan, Bhil, Bhilala, Jat, Bharur, Mahajan); now only Adivasis retain this, for particular occasions.

concepts.name: Geographical Indication registration
concepts.description: The GI 'Bagh Prints of Madhya Pradesh' was recorded under application number 98 in 2008.

concepts.name: Publicly honoured master artisans
concepts.description: Ismail Khatri is described as an eminent printer and national awardee.

concepts.name: Base fabric (cotton, silk and others)
concepts.description: The main raw material is fabric, most commonly cotton; silk-cotton, kosa silk, chiffon, crepe, georgette and mulberry silk are also printed.

concepts.name: Sanchara (rock salt)
concepts.description: 3 kg of sanchara (rock salt) is dissolved in 15 litres of water as one component of the mengni solution.

concepts.name: Mengni (goat dung)
concepts.description: 10 kg of mengni is soaked in water, softened, ground with a brick on a stone and made into a paste; the GI gives the water as 10–15 litres in one passage and 15–20 litres in another.

concepts.name: Arandi ka tel (castor oil)
concepts.description: 1 kg of arandi ka tel (unrefined castor oil) is mixed with sanchara and mengni to make the dhaul solution; the oil is stirred with salt until it curdles.

concepts.name: Harara / harda (Terminalia chebula)
concepts.description: Treating the cloth with harara gives an off-white or off-yellow ground and strengthens the tones of the black and red printed later.

concepts.name: Fitkari (alum) — red mordant
concepts.description: Alum is colourless; it produces red when boiled with alizarine and dhavda flowers.

concepts.name: Hirakasish / iron (ferrous sulphate, iron filings or rust) — black
concepts.description: Black is prepared from ferrous sulphate mixed with tamarind seed powder and glue, cooked in water and stored.

concepts.name: Chiyan (tamarind seed powder) — thickener
concepts.description: Hirakayisha or alum must first be made into a paint-like solution with tamarind seed, with hot water added to reach the required density.

concepts.name: Alizarin (formerly aal root)
concepts.description: Earlier the root of the aal tree was used as a fastening agent; now alizarine has taken its place.

concepts.name: Dhavda ka phool (dhavdi flowers)
concepts.description: Dhavda ka phool is used for shining and fixing in the boiling solution.

concepts.name: Secondary dyes: pomegranate rind, dhavdi leaves, indigo, turmeric
concepts.description: The four basic natural colours used extensively are red, black, khaki and indigo.

concepts.name: Bleaching powder (time-saving substitute)
concepts.description: Sometimes a bit of bleaching powder is added to water and the cloth passed through it, avoiding three to four washes.

concepts.name: Wooden printing blocks (bilal)
concepts.description: Blocks are intricately and deeply carved by block-makers in Pethapur in Gujarat; they are also sourced from Gandhinagar and Jaipur.

concepts.name: Colour tray (palya) with kartali and felt
concepts.description: A wooden tray with cement base (earlier mud) is used; a bamboo mesh (kartali) and a loosely woven woollen blanket are placed on it; for fine blocks a voile cotton layer is added.

concepts.name: Printing table (farsi)
concepts.description: The printing table, farsi, is of red sandstone.

concepts.name: Copper vat on a furnace (bhatti)
concepts.description: Vats are generally copper, fixed on brick and cement furnaces, large enough for 25 single bedcovers.

concepts.name: Rangchalna (stirring sticks)
concepts.description: The cloth must be shifted and turned constantly in the vat with long wooden sticks.

concepts.name: 1. Khara karna (desizing in the river)
concepts.description: The cloth is washed in the river, soaked about 2 hours, beaten on riverside stones, and later beaten on a stone slab to remove starch.

concepts.name: 2. Mengni karna (salt–goat dung–castor oil bath)
concepts.description: Cloth is kept overnight in a dhaul solution of sanchara, mengni and castor oil, washed in flowing river water and dried; the process is repeated three times.

concepts.name: 3. Harara treatment (yellowing)
concepts.description: The day after mengni karna, the fabric is dyed in harara solution for about 10 minutes per lot and dried, turning yellowish.

concepts.name: 4. Preparing mordant pastes
concepts.description: Alum or hirakayisha is first made into a paint-like solution with tamarind seed; hot water adjusts density.

concepts.name: 5. Block printing
concepts.description: Paste is transferred from the tray to the block's raised portions and the designs are transferred very neatly on to the cloth; an expert prints about 5 metres in two to three hours.

concepts.name: 6. Resting / curing the print
concepts.description: The printed material is dried, rolled into bundles and kept away for eight to fifteen days so the colour sets.

concepts.name: 7. Bichalna (river washing of excess colour)
concepts.description: Two people hold the fabric under running water, each piece at least 20 minutes, then beat it against stones to remove residue.

concepts.name: 8. Bhatti (boiling with alizarin and dhavda)
concepts.description: The cloth is boiled in a solution of dhavda ka phool and alizarine; it is during this process that the colour of the prints develops.

concepts.name: 9. Tarai (washing, sprinkling and sun-bleaching)
concepts.description: After drying, the cloth is washed three to four times in the stream; while drying it is repeatedly moistened by spraying water by hand, which helps set the colours (tarai).

concepts.name: 10. Over-dyeing (optional)
concepts.description: Over-dyeing with harara and 5 kg alum (for red) or 5 kg iron sulphate (for black) is done if colour is not bright enough or two shades are required; bichalna and bhatti are then repeated.

concepts.name: Judging the bhatti endpoint and temperature
concepts.description: The workers know from experience when to take the fabric out of the vat.

concepts.name: Adjusting shade by mordant quantity
concepts.description: Shades are obtained by increasing or decreasing hirakayisha or alum.

concepts.name: Printing a colourless mordant
concepts.description: Since alum is colourless, a simple chemical colour is added so the printer can gauge his print; the desired colour appears only after dyeing.

concepts.name: Choosing harara over bahera
concepts.description: Bahera, the alternative to harara, is not used because it gives a blackish tinge.

concepts.name: Correcting stains with pota
concepts.description: Stains from incorrect bichalna cannot be removed except by pota, painting the whole surface black or red with a rag on a stick.

concepts.name: Red and black alternating on white
concepts.description: Bagh layouts are dramatic in the use of black and red alternately on a white background.

concepts.name: Fine geometric repeats
concepts.description: Geometric patterns are interplaced so that the repeated pattern gives a very harmonious appearance.

concepts.name: Named traditional blocks and motif sources
concepts.description: Old block names still in use include Nandana, Laheriya, Attha, Makhi, Zanjiri, Jodhpuri, Jawareya, Molya border, Mungphali, Chaukada, Nareyal, Teekoni and Thuddi.

concepts.name: New designs as variations of old ones
concepts.description: New additions are made every six months as per market demand, with care that the new design is a variation of the old one.

concepts.name: Double dye combinations
concepts.description: A double-dye process yields 'lal per lal' (red on red), 'lal aur kala' and 'lal aur khaki' prints, processing colours sequentially or together.

concepts.name: Bagh red
concepts.description: The signature colour is Bagh red, from tamarind-and-alum pink turned red with alizarin.

concepts.name: Fast black
concepts.description: Alizarin reacts with iron rust to give a bright black colour.

concepts.name: Clear white ground
concepts.description: Washing after printing removes harda completely and makes the fabric white again.

concepts.name: Indirect (mordant) dyeing with alizarin
concepts.description: The dyeing method is indirect: mordants applied during printing react with alizarin to give the final colours.

concepts.name: Iron mordant + alizarin (and tannin) giving black
concepts.description: Alizarin reacts with iron rust to give a bright black colour.

concepts.name: Harara pre-treatment and colour brightness
concepts.description: The yellowish tinge from harda treatment is essential for the brightness of the black and red alizarin colours.

concepts.name: Dependence on flowing river water
concepts.description: Bagh's proximity to the river was an important reason for its choice, as flowing river water is vital to the printing process.

concepts.name: Seasonal river drying and monsoon pause
concepts.description: The Bagh river is dry several times a year, so material has to be taken to the Narmada river, about 30 km away.

concepts.name: Claimed river-water chemistry effect on colour
concepts.description: The chemical composition of the river water is said to be good for the vegetable dyes, giving luminous tones and enhancing red and black.

concepts.name: Sun versus shade drying
concepts.description: Indigo-dyed fabric must be dried in shade or the brightness of the blue changes.

concepts.name: Pressure towards synthetic dyes and shortcuts
concepts.description: Artisans have turned to synthetic colours to save time and meet urban demand.

concepts.name: Does Baghini water chemistry actually affect colour?
concepts.description: The GI text states that the chemical composition of the Bagh river water has proved to be good for the vegetable dyes used for printing at Bagh.

concepts.name: Botanical identity and role of dhavda
concepts.description: Down To Earth identifies the dhavdi flowers boiled with alizarin as Woodfordia fruticosa, the fire flame bush.

concepts.name: Natural or synthetic alizarin today?
concepts.description: Aal root was earlier used; alizarine has taken its place.

concepts.name: When and from where did Bagh printing originate?
concepts.description: There is little written record on this craft and its people.

concepts.name: Bagru hand block printing
concepts.description: Bagru Hand Block Print is mostly printed on cotton, sometimes cotton-silk, mostly with vegetable (natural) dyes, by stamping with wooden blocks.

concepts.name: The Chhipa printer-dyer community of Bagru
concepts.description: The hand printers, known as Chhipa, migrated to Bagru from Sawai Madhopur, Alwar, Jhunjhunu and Sikar districts some 300 years ago, according to the GI dossier citing Mohanty & Mohanty (1983).

concepts.name: Kharadi block-carvers
concepts.description: Turners locally known as Kharadiyas produce the blocks from dried wood such as shisham, mango and teak.

concepts.name: Historical records of Bagru as a printing centre
concepts.description: The GI dossier quotes the Imperial Gazetteer of India (Rajputana, 1908) on Bagru as a small town on the Agra-Ajmer road, and cites Dr G.N. Sharma as saying Bagru was famous for its dyed or printed chintzes.

concepts.name: Caste- and community-specific clientele
concepts.description: Bagru prints are described as rooted in the local folk milieu, with a limited design and colour range tied to traditional caste- and custom-bound end uses.

concepts.name: GI production area: Bagru, Kaladera, Jahota, Jairampura
concepts.description: The geographical area of production is Bagru, Kaladera, Jahota and Jairampura, with Bagru town as the main production centre.

concepts.name: Market change, synthetic dyes and screen-print imitation
concepts.description: Fake screen-printed Bagru textiles were being sold all over India under the Bagru name, motivating GI registration.

concepts.name: Cotton cloth (latha, mulmul, handloom)
concepts.description: Bagru goods use mill-made or handloom latha, grey superfine mulmul, cambric and rezi cloth depending on the item.

concepts.name: Harda (myrobalan, Terminalia chebula)
concepts.description: Washed fabric is treated with myrobalan (harda), which contains tannic acid that attracts the mordants applied by block.

concepts.name: Syahi (fermented iron black)
concepts.description: Syahi is essentially a fermented solution of iron with molasses (jaggery, gur) and gum; with harda it develops a deep black.

concepts.name: Begar (alum mordant paste for red)
concepts.description: Begar paste is the mordant alum which in combination with alizarin develops a rich red colour.

concepts.name: Madder / alizarin dyebath
concepts.description: The red dyebath uses madder (Rubia tinctorum, Rubia manjista), which contains alizarin and purpurin; synthetic alizarin is now used due to shortage.

concepts.name: Dhawai flowers (Woodfordia fruticosa/floribunda)
concepts.description: Dhawai flower (Woodfordia floribunda) is boiled along with alizarin to avoid patches and staining.

concepts.name: Bagru dabu (black-clay resist paste)
concepts.description: Dabu paste is prepared by mixing kali mitti (clay soil), lime, wheat flour and gum in ratios depending on the type of dabu needed.

concepts.name: Sawdust (on wet dabu)
concepts.description: Sawdust absorbs water from the dabu paste and gives an additional layer of resist.

concepts.name: Indigo (neel)
concepts.description: Indigo blue (nil) is extracted from Indigofera tinctoria; synthetic indigo granules are also used nowadays.

concepts.name: Turmeric and pomegranate rind (yellow)
concepts.description: The yellow dye is extracted from haldi (turmeric) and naspal (pomegranate rinds) and is very fugitive.

concepts.name: Alum (fitkari)
concepts.description: Post-mordanting with diluted alum (fitkari) in a big copper vessel makes the yellow dye fast.

concepts.name: Scouring agents: cow dung, soda/soap, sesame oil (telkhar)
concepts.description: Traditionally cow dung was used for scouring; soaps have now replaced it.

concepts.name: Wooden printing block (bunta) — gadh, rekh, datta
concepts.description: Buntas are wooden hand-printing blocks of different shapes with motifs engraved on the bottom face and a wooden handle; the GI names the outline block (rekh) and filler block (dotu), and a maker profile names the background (gudh), outline (rekh) and filler (datta) blocks.

concepts.name: Kalam (carving chisels)
concepts.description: Kalams are steel chisels of different widths and cutting surfaces used by kharadis to engrave motifs on blocks.

concepts.name: Printing table (mej) and low dabu table (pathiya)
concepts.description: Pathiya is a table used for dabu printing, mostly by older printers and women who cannot stand long, and the printer sits on the floor; mej tables are for regular production, with printers walking around the table.

concepts.name: Colour tray with pad (sai / saaj)
concepts.description: Sai are small rectangular containers with a frame and layers of jute and cotton fabric forming a pad to spread colour evenly.

concepts.name: Copper dyeing vessels (tambadi)
concepts.description: Dyeing is carried out in large copper vessels heated by wood fire, with alizarin in small cloth bags dipped in the vessel.

concepts.name: Indigo vat (naand / deep pit vat)
concepts.description: One account gives the indigo vats as 15 feet deep.

concepts.name: Mogri (wooden mallet) and stone slab
concepts.description: Mogri is a wooden mallet used to beat the folds of moist finished cloth.

concepts.name: 1. Scouring (hari sarana / teluni)
concepts.description: Scouring, locally 'hari sarana', removes starch, oil and dust; cloth was left overnight in cow dung and water.

concepts.name: 2. Harda treatment (peela karna)
concepts.description: Harda powder is mixed with water, the cloth submerged, squeezed and dried flat; then folded and beaten to remove excess harda. This is called peela karna.

concepts.name: 3. Mordant printing (chhapai) with syahi and begar
concepts.description: The fabric is printed with two mordants: ferrous syahi from rusted horseshoe nails, and aluminium sulphate begar.

stage.title: 3. Mordant printing (chhapai) with syahi and begar

concepts.name: 4. Ageing / drying (sukhai)
concepts.description: Printed fabric is left at least three to four days so the mordant paste penetrates the fibre; the longer the ageing, the better the result.

concepts.name: 5. Washing off excess mordant (khulai)
concepts.description: The printed fabric is washed in running water to remove excess mordant before dyeing.

concepts.name: 6. Dyeing in alizarin/madder (rangai, bhatti)
concepts.description: The dye reacts with two mordants at two locations on the same print, giving red (with alum) and black (with ferrous).

concepts.name: 7. Resist printing with dabu (dabu chhapai)
concepts.description: Dabu is applied with a wooden block, sawdust is sprinkled over it, and the fabric is dried in the sun before dipping in indigo.

concepts.name: 8. Indigo dyeing (neel rangai)
concepts.description: The cloth is folded like sari pleats, lowered into the tank, and each pleat opened under the liquid so dye reaches evenly.

concepts.name: 9. Yellow over-dyeing by sponging (haldi-naspal putai / potai)
concepts.description: Before yellow dyeing, the fabric is again printed with dabu to retain some blue areas.

stage.title: 9. Yellow over-dyeing by sponging (haldi-naspal putai / potai)

concepts.name: 10. Alum after-mordanting (fitkari rangai)
concepts.description: The fabric is dipped for a few minutes in diluted alum, squeezed, dried flat, then stored folded in dark places for at least 3-4 days so the yellow sets.

concepts.name: 11. Final washing (dhulai) and finishing
concepts.description: The fabric is left in tanks 3-4 hours until the resist softens, then beaten on a flat stone slab where water flows.

concepts.name: Choosing print order and registering blocks by eye
concepts.description: Ferrous outline is printed first because its immediate black impression makes it easy to place the filler block; sometimes the background block is applied before the outline.

concepts.name: Judging alizarin quantity
concepts.description: The quantity of alizarin dye is calculated by the experienced dyer.

concepts.name: Reading and feeding the indigo vat
concepts.description: An expert indigo dyer can tell the state of the vat by its colour and adds exact quantities learnt by experience; there is no written recipe.

concepts.name: Selecting dabu strength for the number of dye trips
concepts.description: Dabu ingredients are mixed in ratios depending on the type of dabu paste needed.

concepts.name: Handling to avoid trapped air and cracked dabu
concepts.description: Air trapped in folds gives patchy dyeing, so an experienced dyer unfolds pleats neatly and gently, also to avoid cracking the dabu.

concepts.name: Off-white / cream ground
concepts.description: The ground colour of Bagru prints is mostly off-white (cream); in Sanganeri prints the background is white.

concepts.name: Two-colour red-and-black palette (syahi-begar)
concepts.description: Traditional Bagru prints are of two colours, red and black; the black imparts a reddish tinge.

concepts.name: Five motif groups; buti, buta, jhar and border
concepts.description: Traditional motifs fall into five groups: flowers, leaves and buds; intertwined tendrils; trellis; figurative; and geometric designs.

concepts.name: Layered block set: background, outline, filler
concepts.description: More colours require more datta blocks.

concepts.name: Dense traditional fields tolerate hand variation
concepts.description: Empty spaces in modern patterns tend to reveal unintentional dye drips.

concepts.name: Syahi-Begar print
concepts.description: Colours obtained with the two mordants in an alizarin bath are red (with alum) and black (with ferrous).

concepts.name: Dabu indigo print
concepts.description: Block printing of plant motifs on a dark indigo background is presented as a peculiarity of Bagru prints.

concepts.name: Bagru green
concepts.description: To turn the fabric green it is yellow-dyed after indigo, with dabu re-printed to retain blue areas.

concepts.name: Two mordants, one dyebath
concepts.description: Dyeing is a process in which the dye reacts with two mordants at two different locations on the same print, giving two different colours.

concepts.name: Harda tannin + syahi iron → black
concepts.description: The tannic acid of myrobalan forms black colour with ferrous syahi.

concepts.name: Dabu as mechanical resist
concepts.description: Dabu acts as a mechanical resist and prevents penetration of dye on areas it covers.

concepts.name: Indigo develops on exposure to air
concepts.description: The fabric is squeezed and opened out to react with atmospheric oxygen, turning reduced indigo into oxidised indigo.

concepts.name: Alum after-mordant fixes fugitive yellows
concepts.description: Turmeric and pomegranate yellow is very fugitive, and post-mordanting with alum makes it fast.

concepts.name: Water and the Sanjaria river
concepts.description: Chhipas came perhaps more for abundant water with excellent properties for dyeing and printing than for royal patronage; the Sanjaria river's perennial stream and sandy bed suited printing.

concepts.name: Strong sun and open drying grounds
concepts.description: Abundant flowing water and a clean sunny bed are important requisites for printing.

concepts.name: Semi-arid climate and monsoon seasonality
concepts.description: The GI dossier's census-2001 data for the production centres give an annual rainfall of 56.64 cm and temperatures from 0.5 to about 48 °C.

concepts.name: Falling water table and effluent
concepts.description: Rains have been less plentiful in recent years and the region's water table has dropped.

concepts.name: Bagru vs Sanganer printing
concepts.description: Bagru prints are deeply rooted in the local folk milieu, contrasting with the courtly sensibility of Sanganer work.

concepts.name: How old is Bagru printing?
concepts.description: There is no authentic record for backdating Bagru's block printing; it is estimated to have been introduced 450 years ago.

concepts.name: What exactly is in begar, and which block is 'datta'?
concepts.description: Begar is the mordant alum.

concepts.name: GI date misreported in popular sources
concepts.description: GI application 183 was filed 10-08-2009 and certificate 150 issued 11-05-2011.

concepts.name: How much current Bagru output uses natural dyes?
concepts.description: Chemical dyes are used in abundance and natural dyes only for specific orders.

concepts.name: Does local water really give Bagru prints their character?
concepts.description: Locally available water is claimed to have excellent properties ideal for dyeing and printing.

concepts.name: Dabu mud-resist block printing
concepts.description: Dabu is mud-resist printing: blocks are dipped in a viscous paste of mud, gum and lime, and resist and dye are applied several times.

concepts.name: Akola village, a Dabu cluster
concepts.description: Akola is a village in Bhopalsagar tehsil, Chittorgarh district, about 52 km west of Chittorgarh.

concepts.name: Chhipa printers and allied dyeing communities
concepts.description: The block printers of Akola are the Chippa community, whose name derives from chhapna, to print.

concepts.name: Name and origin legend
concepts.description: A legend tells of a Rangrez dyer whose mud-stained dhoti left an undyed patch after indigo dyeing.

concepts.name: Antiquity of Dabu (contested dating)
concepts.description: The oldest known Dabu-printed specimen was found in Central Asia, suggesting use in the 8th century AD.

concepts.name: Decline and revival
concepts.description: Rajasthan once had many Dabu clusters; very few remain.

concepts.name: Geographical Indication status
concepts.description: GI application 845, Aakola Dabu Prints, was filed by Udhyam Protsahan Sansthan on 04-03-2022 and its status is Pre Examination.

concepts.name: Phetiya, nangna and community dress
concepts.description: A fetiya was made from one long Dabu-printed cloth of 8-12 m with a single line of stitching, worn by Jat, Gadariya and Gujjar women, usually with a bandhej lugda.

concepts.name: Other Dabu centres
concepts.description: Dabu printing was also practised in Tarapur, Bhilwara and Pahuna.

concepts.name: Mud / black clay (kali mitti)
concepts.description: Mud is dug from a dry pond and soaked overnight in a separate tank.

concepts.name: Lime (chuna, calcium hydroxide)
concepts.description: The resist paste is mud, gum and lime.

concepts.name: Natural gum (gond)
concepts.description: Gum from acacia or babul seeds acts as the binder.

concepts.name: Wheat chaff / beedan (insect-eaten wheat flour)
concepts.description: The paste is made with gum, mud and waste wheat chaff.

concepts.name: Sugarcane molasses (Deesa recipe)
concepts.description: The Deesa paste is a mix of river-bed silt, local gum, lime, sugarcane molasses and water.

concepts.name: Recipe variants: kalidar, dolidar, gawarvali, rait
concepts.description: Three resists are used: chuna/lime the weakest for fine outlines, mitti/mud for repeated indigo immersion, rait/sand the strongest for absorbent colours like pomegranate and ferrous.

concepts.name: Sawdust
concepts.description: White areas stamped with paste are immediately covered with sawdust to prevent the wet clay smudging.

concepts.name: Indigo
concepts.description: In Gaatha's origin story, the parts of the cloth where earth had rested took no dye in the indigo vat and kept their original colour.

concepts.name: Reds: alizarin, now naphthol with red salt
concepts.description: Alizarin (red) was later replaced by naphthol.

concepts.name: Cotton cloth
concepts.description: Cotton fabric of 20x20 count is sourced from Kishangarh.

concepts.name: Tar, oil and rogan resist (modern Akola substitute)
concepts.description: The resist is now a mixture of tar, oil and rogan; earlier a mud paste was used.

concepts.name: Harda (myrobalan), alum and iron
concepts.description: At Bagru, scoured cloth is washed in powdered harda and water, giving a yellow tint; harda's tannic acid acts as a mordant for the iron of the black printing colour.

concepts.name: Carved wooden printing blocks
concepts.description: Block carvers in the village make the wooden blocks.

concepts.name: Printing table
concepts.description: Small wooden printing tables of about 150 cm x 60 cm are used.

concepts.name: Indigo vat and dyeing trays
concepts.description: Dyeing trays of wood or plastic are used.

concepts.name: Straining cloth and mardia pot
concepts.description: The paste is strained before use.

concepts.name: Boilers for tar removal
concepts.description: Large kadhai-like boilers for removing tar were set up with government support.

concepts.name: Collecting and soaking the mud
concepts.description: Mud is dug from a dry pond and soaked overnight in a separate tank.

concepts.name: Preparing the resist paste
concepts.description: The paste is kneaded by stamping over several days, then strained before use.

concepts.name: Washing / scouring the cloth
concepts.description: The fabric is first washed to remove impurities that could block dyeing.

concepts.name: Optional pre-printing of colour (naphthol red)
concepts.description: Naphthol is printed on areas to be red, sun-dried, then dipped in red salt.

concepts.name: Block-printing the resist
concepts.description: Craftsmen dip the blocks into a viscous paste of mud, gum and lime; the method's name comes from dabaana, to press.

concepts.name: Dusting the wet resist
concepts.description: Paste areas are immediately covered with sawdust to prevent smudging.

concepts.name: Sun-drying the resist
concepts.description: The fabric is sun-dried until the paste hardens.

concepts.name: Dip-dyeing (usually indigo)
concepts.description: The cloth is dip-dyed after the paste hardens.

concepts.name: Airing and drying
concepts.description: The cloth turns green, then deepens to indigo as it oxidises in air.

concepts.name: Washing off the resist
concepts.description: The fabric is washed to remove paste and excess dye.

concepts.name: Repeating resist-dye cycles (double/triple dabu)
concepts.description: The resist-and-dye sequence is repeated through a dye bath for each colour needed.

concepts.name: Choosing the resist recipe for the job
concepts.description: Lime is used for fine outlines, mud for repeated indigo immersion, and sand for absorbent colours such as pomegranate and ferrous dyes.

concepts.name: Working the paste to a viscous consistency
concepts.description: The paste is kneaded by stamping over several days and strained before use.

concepts.name: Dusting immediately and drying fully before dyeing
concepts.description: The paste is immediately covered with sawdust to keep the wet clay from smudging, and sun-dried until hard before dip-dyeing.

concepts.name: Judging dips and cycles for the shade
concepts.description: The indigo dip is repeated until the required shade is reached.

concepts.name: Mud or tar for fine designs
concepts.description: Tar replaced mud for finer designs because mud mostly cracked and changed the look.

concepts.name: Motifs drawn from nature and surroundings
concepts.description: Motifs are picked from nature and surrounding elements and crafted onto wooden blocks.

concepts.name: Named Akola motifs (Lal Titri, Kahma, Dholika, Kantedar)
concepts.description: Four main motifs survive: Kahma, Lal Titri, Dholika and Kantedar.

concepts.name: Reserving light motifs on a dyed ground
concepts.description: In Gaatha's origin story, where earth rested on the cloth the dye did not take, and that part kept its original colour, like stars in an indigo sky.

concepts.name: Layered colour through successive resists
concepts.description: Resist and dye applied several times create different ground and motif shades.

concepts.name: Patterns tied to communities and garments
concepts.description: Phetia was worn by Jat and Chaudhury women and nangna by Gujjar women.

concepts.name: Undyed motifs on an indigo ground
concepts.description: In Gaatha's origin story, the part of the cloth where earth had rested kept its original colour after the indigo vat.

concepts.name: Crackle / veining effect
concepts.description: The result shows uneven cracks, and the stages of applying mud-resist, dyeing and washing are said to produce elegant veining.

concepts.name: Multi-tone layered cloth (blue, red, brown)
concepts.description: Repeated resist and dyeing build shades of soil brown and neela (indigo).

concepts.name: Why a mud resist suits a cold indigo vat
concepts.description: Clay resist can only be used with indigo because the vat is cold and submersion quick, which prevents the clay washing off.

concepts.name: Crack formation lets dye penetrate the resist
concepts.description: Dyes may enter the fabric where the mud cracks.

concepts.name: Dusting powder dries the wet paste quickly
concepts.description: Dusting with beden dries the paste quickly and keeps it from smudging.

concepts.name: Developing naphthol red with red salt
concepts.description: Dipping in red salt reacts with the naphthol to produce a bright red.

concepts.name: Strong sun and arid climate
concepts.description: The fabric is sun-dried until the paste hardens.

concepts.name: River water for washing (Beduch)
concepts.description: Water comes from the Beduch river, plus hand pumps and tube wells.

concepts.name: Groundwater pollution and workplace hazards
concepts.description: Heated tar fumes and ash dust are hazardous to printers.

concepts.name: What exactly is in the Dabu paste?
concepts.description: Paste is mud, gum and lime.

concepts.name: Is Akola Dabu still mud-based?
concepts.description: The resist is now tar, oil and rogan; earlier a mud paste was used.

concepts.name: Age, district and community attribution
concepts.description: Global InCH places Akola in Udaipur district.

concepts.name: GI status of Akola Dabu
concepts.description: Application 845 status is Pre Examination.

concepts.name: Machilipatnam (Pedana) block-printed Kalamkari
concepts.description: Machilipatnam Kalamkari is a registered Geographical Indication (application no. 90) filed by the Vegetable Hand-block Kalamkari Printers Association, Pedana, for handicraft goods in classes 24, 25 and 27.

concepts.name: GI production area: Pedana and neighbouring villages
concepts.description: Production of Machilipatnam Kalamkari is geographically limited to Pedana town and its neighbouring villages Machilipatnam, Polavaram and Kappaladoddi in Guduru mandal, Krishna district.

concepts.name: Golconda patronage and the port of Masulipatnam
concepts.description: The rulers at Golconda patronised kalamkari of Masulipatnam (now Machilipatnam) during the 16th and 17th centuries; textiles were made for the Sultanate and Persia/Iran and customised to Islamic taste.

concepts.name: Export to Persia/Iran
concepts.description: An 1879 Machilipatnam dress fabric was probably made for export to Iran; its Persian inscription names the trader and calls the textile qalamkar, a printed imitation of hand-drawn kalamkari.

concepts.name: Coromandel chintz and the European trade
concepts.description: Chintz was imported in large quantities into Britain and the Netherlands in the 17th and 18th centuries, and its mordant/resist techniques are particularly associated with the Coromandel Coast.

concepts.name: Shift from pen (kalam) to block
concepts.description: Kalams were replaced by blocks in the nineteenth century.

concepts.name: Geographical Indication registration
concepts.description: Application filed 16-04-2007, published in journal Supplementary 1 (available 24-03-2008), certificate no. 71 dated 10-07-2008, valid up to 15-04-2027.

concepts.name: Producer communities and karkhana organisation
concepts.description: The main castes engaged are Devangas, Padmasalis, Kannebhaktulu and Senapathalu; dyers and printers belonged to Hindu or Muslim faiths; blocks were made by specialist block makers, sometimes by printers themselves.

concepts.name: Unbleached cotton (kora long cloth)
concepts.description: The base is kora (unbleached) long cloth of 20 or 60 counts.

concepts.name: Myrobalan (karakkaya)
concepts.description: Myrobalan solution is prepared from karakkaya, pounded, boiled at least 2.5 hours, filtered, and kept overnight; the cloth dipped in it turns yellowish.

concepts.name: Kasim (iron acetate black mordant)
concepts.description: Iron acetate (kasim in Telugu) is made from salt water, jaggery, iron strips and paddy husk; the strips are smouldered overnight, cleaned and fermented with jaggery-salt solution in a covered stone pot sunk 90% below ground.

concepts.name: Alum (karam)
concepts.description: Alum (karam in Telugu) is pounded, boiled in water until reduced to half, and iron implements are avoided because iron darkens the colour.

concepts.name: Alum
concepts.description: The alum solution for the fixing dip is made by adding cool water to pounded alum crystals.

concepts.name: Alizarin, madder and chay root (red dye)
concepts.description: Madder (Rubia) and chay (Oldenlandia umbellata) were highly estimated as fine sources of red in the south.

concepts.name: Indigo
concepts.description: Indigo is obtained from indigo cakes and mixed with rice starch, not gum, for printing; indigo does not require any mordant so it is printed directly.

concepts.name: Buffalo milk
concepts.description: Buffalo milk (5 L to 6 kg rice) is stirred into rice starch to stiffen it and help it spread evenly; fresh milk in the starch prevents colours from running.

concepts.name: Cow or buffalo dung
concepts.description: Unbleached cloth is soaked 5–10 minutes in buffalo or cow dung and water, kept wet overnight, washed in flowing water and sun-dried; nowadays sometimes dipped once as cleansing rather than bleaching.

concepts.name: Gum (printing thickener)
concepts.description: Gum-mixed black colour is printed, and gum is washed out with loose colour in flowing water.

concepts.name: Rice starch (ganji)
concepts.description: For yellow, the fabric is dipped in prepared starch (boiled rice water) which prevents diffusion of yellow and seepage to the reverse.

concepts.name: Dye-bath plant additives (jajaku/gaja leaves, moduga, pomegranate)
concepts.description: Jajaku leaves are added with alizarin and act as a carrier that hastens dyeing; moduga and anar shift the colour toward orange.

concepts.name: Beeswax (resist)
concepts.description: Beeswax is a raw material, melted in broken pots.

concepts.name: Carved wooden printing blocks
concepts.description: A pen drawing is transferred to carved teakwood blocks and each colour gets its own block.

concepts.name: Printing table with gunny and damp cloth
concepts.description: Printing is done on a long wooden table covered with gunny cloth and a damp cloth; the damp under-surface prevents slipping.

concepts.name: Mordant/colour printing pad (tray)
concepts.description: The printing pad is a rectangular teak tray with bamboo separators, a sponge layer and a woollen or gunny cover acting as a blotter.

concepts.name: Boiling vessels and fire-places
concepts.description: A copper pot on a brick fireplace is used to boil the cloth in alizarin solution; larger copper pots for boiling are among the tools.

concepts.name: Earthen pot for kasim
concepts.description: The cleaned iron strips are placed in a barrel-shaped stone pot, securely covered, 90 per cent below ground level.

concepts.name: Date-palm brush and kalam
concepts.description: The yellow stage is the only stage where a brush made of date-palm stick is used.

concepts.name: Design drawing and block carving
concepts.description: Block making is the first stage of production.

concepts.name: Scouring / dung bleaching
concepts.description: Grey cloth is soaked in dung and water, kept wet overnight, washed in flowing water, spread over waterweed and dried in the sun.

concepts.name: Myrobalan (karakkaya) treatment
concepts.description: The bleached cloth is dipped in myrobalan solution, squeezed and dried in the sun.

concepts.name: Printing iron mordant (kasim) outlines
concepts.description: Gum-mixed black colour is printed with a wooden block, usually to outline the design.

concepts.name: Printing alum mordant (karam)
concepts.description: Alum-based red paste is block-printed where red is needed.

concepts.name: Drying / curing the printed mordants
concepts.description: After block printing the cloth is kept two to three days until dried.

concepts.name: Degumming wash in flowing water
concepts.description: The cloth is washed in flowing water to remove gum and unwanted mordant so colour does not develop in unwanted areas; after washing for one hour it is dried in the sun.

concepts.name: Dye-bath boiling (red development)
concepts.description: The mordant-printed fabric is submerged and boiled for an hour and a half with alizarin and jajaku leaves, swirled for even permeation.

concepts.name: Squeezing and sun-drying after dyeing
concepts.description: After red has developed the cloth is taken out, squeezed and dried in the sun.

concepts.name: Second printing: yellow, green, grey, indigo
concepts.description: A second printing applies yellow, green, pink, grey and indigo; yellow is brushed on with a date-palm stick over starched cloth.

stage.title: Second printing: yellow, green, grey, indigo

concepts.name: Alum fixing dip
concepts.description: The fabric is submerged in alum solution; the excess yellow runs off and all colours are fixed.

concepts.name: Soaping and final sun-drying
concepts.description: The last stage is washing with soap, after which the cloth is dried in the sun.

concepts.name: Choosing print order by background colour
concepts.description: The two printing stages might reverse depending on the colour; if the background is indigo or indigo-green it is printed last.

concepts.name: Judging boiling time and bath additives for shade
concepts.description: The amount of time the cloth is kept in water determines the shade.

concepts.name: Varying alum concentration for shades of red
concepts.description: Different alum concentrations produce more shades.

concepts.name: Keeping printed cloth dry before washing
concepts.description: Printed cloth must stay dry since moisture makes the colours spread.

concepts.name: Avoiding iron utensils with alum
concepts.description: A mixture of iron in any form leads to darkening of the colour, so iron implements and utensils are avoided.

concepts.name: Scheduling work around weather
concepts.description: The entire process takes almost two months; nature should be favourable, and progress depends entirely on nature.

concepts.name: Persian-influenced floral and architectural motifs
concepts.description: Persian influence shows in ornamental birds, flowers, creepers and mehrabs or archways; border patterns and a repetitive floral field displaced the early designs.

concepts.name: Black outline, then colour fills — one block per colour
concepts.description: Each colour gets its own block.

concepts.name: Mordant-dye palette: black, red, blue, yellow, green
concepts.description: Kalamkari cottons are made in black, red, blue, yellow and green.

concepts.name: Designing to market taste
concepts.description: Designs catered to Persian taste, and Dutch and English demand also influenced design.

concepts.name: Colourfast printed textiles and products
concepts.description: Products include block-printed sarees, rugs, hand towels, door covers, bed covers and clothing material.

concepts.name: Red, black and pinkish ground from one dye bath
concepts.description: Red develops from alum and alizarin, alizarin also fixes the black, and portions not treated with alum imbibe a pinkish colour.

concepts.name: Screen-printed imitation and market pressure
concepts.description: Screen-printed kalamkari uses chemical colours, is faster and cheaper, and is hard to distinguish at first sight.

concepts.name: Myrobalan tannin as mordant receptor
