concepts.description: The tannin in myrobalan reacts with iron salt to produce black; with alum it improves fastness of the red dye; it helps cotton absorb iron and alum salts more evenly.

concepts.name: Mordant-selective colour development in one bath
concepts.description: Red areas were painted with an alum mordant and black with an iron mordant, which help the dyes fix and give fast colours.

concepts.name: Indigo needs no mordant
concepts.description: Indigo needs no mordant, so wax resist protected areas not to be blue before dipping in the vat.

concepts.name: Buffalo-milk fat limits dye bleeding (practitioner explanation)
concepts.description: Buffalo milk fat penetrates deep into the fabric which prevents dyes from spreading.

concepts.name: Flowing water for washing (canal/pond)
concepts.description: Washing of cotton fabrics at Machilipatnam is done at the Kalia Canal.

concepts.name: Sunlight and dry weather
concepts.description: Cloth is sun-dried after bleaching, myrobalan, washing, dyeing and soaping; progress depends entirely on nature.

concepts.name: Coromandel soil, water and dye plants
concepts.description: These techniques are associated with the Coromandel Coast because local soil, water and dye plants provided a favourable combination of chemicals.

concepts.name: Water pollution from chemical printing
concepts.description: Chemical effluents from washing screen-printed fabric reportedly pollute water; the Krishna District Collector sent notices to those using chemical colours, warning them of action.

concepts.name: Machilipatnam (block) vs Srikalahasti (pen) kalamkari
concepts.description: Srikalahasti style is freehand pen drawing with Hindu mythological stories, mostly for temple cloths; Machilipatnam is hand-block printed with Persian motifs.

concepts.name: Is alum used for red at Machilipatnam?
concepts.description: Unlike Srikalahasti, alum solution is not used here for the red colour.

concepts.name: Copper or iron boiling vessels?
concepts.description: Copper pots are used for boiling and iron utensils are avoided with alum.

concepts.name: Order of iron vs alum printing
concepts.description: The printing of iron mordant precedes that of alum.

concepts.name: GI registration year: 2008, 2012 or 2013?
concepts.description: Certificate no. 71 dated 10-07-2008.

concepts.name: Myrobalan plant part and buffalo-milk step
concepts.description: Myrobalan solution is prepared from the dried flowers called karakkaya.

concepts.name: Total duration and number of steps
concepts.description: Hand block printing takes a minimum of 10 steps.

concepts.name: Natural red roots vs synthetic alizarin today
concepts.description: Alizarin is brought from Mumbai.

concepts.name: Srikalahasti kalamkari (the hand-painted style)
concepts.description: The Srikalahasti style of kalamkari is drawn freehand with a pen, with motifs and stories from Hindu mythology.

concepts.name: Sanganeri hand block printing
concepts.description: The GI specification gives the base colour of Sanganeri hand block prints as white, with delicate floral motifs and necessarily repetitive designs.

concepts.name: Sanganer town and the GI production area
concepts.description: The geographical area of production is mainly Sanganer town, 16 km from Jaipur and headquarters of Sanganer tehsil, together with nearby villages.

concepts.name: Founding of Sanganer (early 16th century)
concepts.description: Sanganer was founded by the Kachhwaha prince Sangaji in the early 16th century; the GI application (citing Hanuman Sharma) adds that he was the son of Prithviraj of Amber.

concepts.name: Migration of printers and Jaipur royal patronage
concepts.description: Oral tradition, said to be confirmed by archival sources, holds that Sawai Jai Singh invited craftsmen to Jaipur, including printers from Gujarat; Malwa craftsmen are conjectured too.

concepts.name: Archival evidence from the 18th and 19th centuries
concepts.description: East India Company records of the 16th and 17th centuries do not name Sanganer; dastur-al-amal reports of 1703 and rangkhana records of 1727 describe taxes on printed fabrics.

concepts.name: Chintz, exhibitions and museum collections
concepts.description: A length of Sanganer block-printed cotton, about 1850, was purchased from the Great Exhibition of 1851.

concepts.name: Chhipa printers
concepts.description: The art and skill are limited to the Chhipa community, who acquired them from parents and grandparents over generations.

concepts.name: Kharadi block-makers
concepts.description: Turners locally known as Kharadis carve the blocks from dried wood of shisham, gurjan, mango and teak.

concepts.name: Screen printing, synthetic dyes and revival (1960s onward)
concepts.description: Screen printing entered Sanganer around 1960 through Khatri migrants from Mirpur and Sind, and many printing families adopted mill cloth, synthetic dyes and screens.

concepts.name: Geographical Indication registration and its use
concepts.description: Sanganeri Hand Block Printing (application 147) appears in the GI Registry list in the section for April 2009 to March 2010.

concepts.name: Base fabric: cotton, mulmul and silk
concepts.description: Sanganeri textiles are mostly printed on cotton and sometimes on cotton-silk; safas are printed on a fine fabric called mulmul.

concepts.name: Harda (myrobalan)
concepts.description: Washed fabric is treated with myrobalan (harda), which contains tannic acid that attracts the mordants applied with wooden blocks.

concepts.name: Syahi (fermented iron black)
concepts.description: Syahi is a fermented solution of iron with jaggery (gur) and gum, and develops a deep black in combination with harda.

concepts.name: Begar (alum mordant paste)
concepts.description: Begar paste is the alum mordant which, combined with alizarine, develops a rich red colour.

concepts.name: Madder / alizarin dye bath
concepts.description: The red bath is prepared from madder (Rubia manjista), containing alizarin and purpurin; synthetic alizarine is now used due to a shortage of the vegetable dye.

concepts.name: Dhawai flowers (dyeing auxiliary)
concepts.description: Alizarine and dhawai flowers are mixed in specific ratios in water for the red bath.

concepts.name: Dabu (mud resist paste)
concepts.description: Dabu paste is prepared by mixing kali mitti, lime, wheat flour and gum in ratios that depend on the type of dabu needed.

concepts.name: Sawdust (on wet dabu)
concepts.description: Sawdust sprinkled over dabu absorbs water from the paste and gives additional layers of resist.

concepts.name: Indigo (neel)
concepts.description: Indigo blue (nil) is extracted from Indigofera tinctoria; nowadays synthetic indigo granules are used.

concepts.name: Turmeric and pomegranate-rind yellow
concepts.description: The yellow dye is extracted from haldi (turmeric) and naspal (pomegranate rind) and is very fugitive.

concepts.name: Alum (fitkari)
concepts.description: The fabric is printed with two mordants: ferrous (syahi) and aluminium sulphate (begar).

concepts.name: Cow dung
concepts.description: Traditionally cow dung was used for scouring, but soaps have now replaced it because the method is tedious and slow.

concepts.name: Synthetic dyes and pigments (present-day)
concepts.description: Natural and/or synthetic azo-free dyes are mostly used.

concepts.name: Bunta (carved wooden printing block)
concepts.description: Buntas are wooden blocks of various shapes with motifs engraved on the bottom face and a wooden handle on top that the printer strikes.

concepts.name: Block set: rekh (outline), datta (filler) and background blocks
concepts.description: The iron mordant is usually printed with the outline block (rekh), and another printer then registers the filler block (datta) with begar.

concepts.name: Printing table (patia) with padded surface
concepts.description: Fabric is spread over a low bench covered with a thick pad of several layers of heavy cloth, and the printer squats in front of it.

concepts.name: Colour tray with jute-and-cotton pad
concepts.description: A frame and layers of jute and cotton fabric inside the colour container spread the colour evenly and form a pad for the block impression.

concepts.name: Kalam (block-carving chisels)
concepts.description: Kalams are steel chisels of different widths and cutting surfaces used by Kharadis to engrave motifs on the blocks.

concepts.name: Copper dye vessel over a wood-fired furnace
concepts.description: Dyeing is carried out in large copper vessels heated by wood fire, with the alizarin placed in small cloth bags.

concepts.name: Mogri (wooden mallet)
concepts.description: The mogri, a wooden mallet, is used in some cases to beat the folds of moist finished cloth.

concepts.name: Indigo vat (tank)
concepts.description: Starting a new indigo tank is tedious and complicated, but once ready it is kept alive by adding indigo, lime and jaggery.

concepts.name: Block carving (preparatory)
concepts.description: Block carving proceeds through ghisai (smoothing), chakai (design transfer), khudai (carving), dabana (levelling the background), chilai (smoothing the sides) and fixing the hatha handle.

concepts.name: 1. Scouring and bleaching the grey cloth
concepts.description: Cloth is scoured to remove starch, oil and dust for good, even penetration of colours.

stage.title: 1. Scouring and bleaching the grey cloth

concepts.name: 2. Harda pre-treatment (peela karna)
concepts.description: Harda powder is mixed with water; the cloth is submerged, squeezed, dried flat, then folded and beaten with a mallet; this is called peela karna.

concepts.name: 3. Printing the mordants (chhapai)
concepts.description: The block is pressed onto a dye-saturated pad and stamped on the fabric; each colour has a separate pan.

concepts.name: 4. Ageing (sukhai)
concepts.description: Printed fabric is left at least three to four days so the mordant paste penetrates the fibre; the longer the ageing, the better the result.

concepts.name: 5. Washing off excess mordant (khulai)
concepts.description: Printed fabric is washed in running water to remove excess mordants before dyeing.

concepts.name: 6. Alizarin / madder dyeing (rangai)
concepts.description: The dye reacts with two mordants at two locations on the same print, giving red with alum and black with ferrous.

concepts.name: 7. Sun-bleaching (tapai)
concepts.description: Alizarin over-dyes the ground to an off-white or yellow tinge, so the fabric is sun-bleached to whiten the ground again.

concepts.name: 8. Dabu resist printing
concepts.description: Dabu is applied with a wooden block, sawdust is sprinkled over it, and the fabric is sun-dried before the indigo tanks.

concepts.name: 9. Indigo dyeing (neel rangai)
concepts.description: Cloth folded like sari pleats is lowered into the tank and opened under the liquid; it is then taken out and opened to react with atmospheric oxygen.

concepts.name: 10. Yellow dyeing by mopping (haldi naspal putai)
concepts.description: Four persons hold the cloth at the corners while a fifth rubs on turmeric and pomegranate-rind dye with a loose-woven woollen cloth used as a sponge.

stage.title: 10. Yellow dyeing by mopping (haldi naspal putai)

concepts.name: 11. Alum post-mordanting (fitkari rangai)
concepts.description: Fabric is dipped for a few minutes in a copper vessel of water and diluted alum, squeezed and dried flat.

concepts.name: 12. Final washing (dhulai)
concepts.description: Fabric is left in big tanks for at least 3 to 4 hours until the resist paste becomes smooth, then beaten on a flat stone slab to remove paste and excess dye.

concepts.name: Choosing the block order for registration
concepts.description: Ferrous is usually printed with the outline block because it immediately shows a black impression, so another printer can easily place the filler block.

concepts.name: Judging dye quantities and recipe ratios
concepts.description: The quantity of alizarin dye is calculated by the experienced dyer.

concepts.name: Reading and feeding the indigo vat
concepts.description: An expert indigo dyer can tell the state of the dye by the colour of the vat and adds ingredients by experience.

concepts.name: Handling cloth to avoid patchy indigo and cracked dabu
concepts.description: Air trapped in folds or pleats gives patchy dyeing, so the dyer opens each pleat neatly and gently under the liquid, avoiding cracking of the dabu.

concepts.name: Deciding how long to age printed cloth
concepts.description: Printed fabric is aged at least three to four days, and longer ageing gives a better result.

concepts.name: Matching motifs and colours to patron and occasion
concepts.description: Motifs had to suit the occasion, location and requirements of the patrons who commissioned the textiles.

concepts.name: Motif vocabulary: buti, buta, jhar/jaal and bel
concepts.description: Sanganeri design forms are known as butis, butas, jhar and border, and all GI textiles carry buti, buta or jhar or a combination.

concepts.name: Fine, stylised florals on a white ground
concepts.description: Motifs can be flowers, leaves and buds, intertwisted tendrils, figurative designs or geometric designs; more than a hundred traditional designs are used.

concepts.name: Harmonising several designs in one cloth
concepts.description: A special feature of Sanganer prints is the use of a variety of designs in the same cloth, beautifully harmonised.

concepts.name: Design categories by user and use
concepts.description: Syahi-begar black and red designs on white cloth were used for safa turbans or angochha shawls of local men; buti florals on white or soft grounds were favoured by the Jaipur court.

concepts.name: Clear white ground with red and black design
concepts.description: Sanganeri saris have red and black as the two main colours with shades of yellow, brown, indigo, blue and green.

concepts.name: Design equally visible on the reverse
concepts.description: The print design is equally vividly seen on the underside of the cloth.

concepts.name: Fast, bright colours ('colours of Sanganer')
concepts.description: Sanganer was known for its bright and fast dyes; a collection of sayings dated 1796 refers to the 'colours of Sanganer'.

concepts.name: Green by overdyeing indigo with yellow
concepts.description: To make green, indigo-dyed fabric goes on to yellow dyeing, with dabu printed first to retain some blue areas.

concepts.name: Product range
concepts.description: Products include saris, chintz yardage for ghagharas, salwar suits with dupattas, safas and home furnishings such as bedspreads, quilts and curtains.

concepts.name: One dye bath, two colours: iron and alum mordants
concepts.description: The dye reacts with two mordants at two locations on the same print, giving red with alum and black with ferrous.

concepts.name: Sun-bleaching explained as alkali plus solar heat
concepts.description: The interaction of alkali from cow dung and thermal heat from sun rays bleaches the ground colour white again.

concepts.name: Dabu as a mechanical resist
concepts.description: Dabu acts as a mechanical resist and prevents the penetration of dye on covered areas.

concepts.name: Indigo: reduced in the vat, oxidised in air, built up by repeated dips
concepts.description: Fabric is opened out to react with atmospheric oxygen and turn reduced indigo into oxidised indigo.

concepts.name: River and running water
concepts.description: Oral tradition says chhipa families moved their work to places with space and running water near Jaipur; Sanganer's riverbanks were ideal.

concepts.name: Strong sun, open ground and semi-arid climate
concepts.description: Annual rainfall is 556 mm, and district temperatures range from 3 to 50 degrees Celsius.

concepts.name: Dyeing effluent, the Amanishah Nallah and groundwater
concepts.description: Wastewater from Sanganer dyeing and printing units is high in sodium, chloride and sulfate, with copper, chromium and iron, and enters the Amanishah Nallah untreated.

concepts.name: When did printing begin at Sanganer?
concepts.description: No record of a Sanganer printing unit is traced before the early 18th century (the earliest cited are dastur-al-amal reports of 1703); the GI applicant infers printing was established by then.

concepts.name: Who founded Sanganer?
concepts.description: Sanganer was founded by Sangaji, son of Prithviraj of Amber.

concepts.name: GI registration year: 2009 or 2010?
concepts.description: Application 147 is listed in the registry section for April 2009 to March 2010.

concepts.name: Which river, and does the water really shape the colours?
concepts.description: The riverbanks of the river Dhoondh were an asset to the dyers and bleachers.

concepts.name: How much present-day Sanganeri printing is natural-dyed, and what counts as 'natural'?
concepts.description: Synthetic alizarine is now used because of a shortage of vegetable alizarine, and synthetic indigo granules from the market are used nowadays.

concepts.name: How much of the pollution comes from block printing, and is effluent treated?
concepts.description: Dyeing and printing units collectively pollute the Amanishah Nallah and groundwater.

concepts.name: Aluminium (alum) mordant complexation
concepts.description: Mordants are metal salts that form an insoluble complex with dye molecules.

concepts.name: Alizarin (madder) metal-lake formation
concepts.description: The red colour complex is a lake of alizarin, aluminium and calcium; other hydroxy-anthraquinone dyes also complex.

concepts.name: Iron-tannin black and iron-catalysed fibre degradation
concepts.description: Iron mordant and tannins have long been combined to achieve deep blacks, greys and browns.

concepts.name: Indigo vat reduction and air re-oxidation
concepts.description: Indigo is not soluble in water whereas leucoindigo is; indigo is transformed to leucoindigo by indigo-reducing bacteria.

concepts.name: Mud-resist barrier and crackle
concepts.description: The most common resist for indigo today is a mud paste called Dabu, which often shows characteristic crack lines where the dye penetrated cracks in the resist.

concepts.name: Tannin (myrobalan) pre-mordanting of cotton
concepts.description: Tannins are polyphenolic compounds with many -OH groups that chelate metals; they were known to improve colour uptake by attracting more mordant and probably served as a secondary mordant attracting aluminium.

concepts.name: Sun bleaching of the ground
concepts.description: Cleaning treatments are repeated several times, interspersed with laying the cloth in the sun to be bleached by oxidation.

concepts.name: Thickened print-paste rheology
concepts.description: Sharpness, penetration, levelness, colour yield and retained white ground heavily rely on print-paste viscosity and rheological behaviour; viscosity depends on the thickener.

concepts.name: Scouring and desizing of cotton
concepts.description: Warp threads are coated with a sizing agent, most commonly starch, which must be removed before dyeing and finishing.

concepts.name: Alum (potassium aluminium sulfate)
concepts.description: Alum is potassium aluminium sulfate; aluminium acetate made as 'red liquor' was also used and is supposed to be better for cellulosic fibres.

concepts.name: Iron acetate solution
concepts.description: Iron acetate made of fermented scrap iron is printed as a paste.

concepts.name: Madder-family red dyes / alizarin
concepts.description: Indian red dyes are from the Rubiaceae (Morinda citrifolia/Al, Rubia cordifolia/munjeet, chay root) and differ chemically from Rubia tinctorum; synthetic alizarin is now common.

concepts.name: Indigo
concepts.description: Indigo is not soluble in water and must be reduced to leucoindigo to dye.

concepts.name: Myrobalan (harde, Terminalia chebula fruit)
concepts.description: Tannins in Terminalia chebula fruit are predominantly hydrolysable tannins: gallotannins, ellagitannins and chebulic ellagitannins.

concepts.name: Cotton (cellulose) cloth
concepts.description: Raw cotton carries hydrophobic waxes, fats and pectins; most natural dyes have affinity for protein rather than cellulose fibres.

concepts.name: Natural gum thickener
concepts.description: Dabu resist paste contains a local natural gum.

concepts.name: Lime (calcium hydroxide)
concepts.description: In the traditional Japanese procedure, the indigo fermentation mixture is maintained above pH 10.3-10.5 by adding lime hydrate.

concepts.name: Clay / river silt (resist base)
concepts.description: Dabu paste is based on silt from a dried river bed.

concepts.name: Mordant red
concepts.description: Chay root with alum mordant gives red.

concepts.name: Iron black / dark purple
concepts.description: Chay root with iron mordant gives black.

concepts.name: Indigo blue
concepts.description: On exposure to air the dye oxidises to the insoluble blue form adhering to the fibres.

concepts.name: Crackle lines in resisted areas
concepts.description: Dabu-resisted cloth often shows crack lines where dye penetrated cracks in the resist.

concepts.name: What complex gives the black/purple of iron under Indian red dyes?
concepts.description: Chay with iron mordant gives black.

concepts.name: Photochemistry of traditional sun bleaching
concepts.description: Sun exposure bleaches the cloth by oxidation.

concepts.name: Scoured cotton cloth
concepts.description: Scoured and washed cotton cloth prepared as the printing ground.

concepts.name: Low affinity of cellulose for metal ions
concepts.description: Cellulose lacks the acidic and basic side groups of protein fibres, so it binds metal mordant ions poorly on its own.

concepts.name: Harda (myrobalan) pre-treatment
concepts.description: The cloth is steeped in a bath of ground harda (myrobalan, fruit of Terminalia chebula) and dried before printing.

concepts.name: Cloth turns pale yellow
concepts.description: After the harda bath the cloth takes on a pale yellowish tint.

concepts.name: Tannins adsorbed on the fibre supply metal-binding groups
concepts.description: Hydrolysable tannins from harda adsorb onto cellulose; their phenolic hydroxyl groups can complex metal ions, acting as a bridge between fibre and mordant.

concepts.name: More mordant fixed where printed
concepts.description: The tannin-treated cotton retains more of the printed metal mordant, allowing deeper, faster colours.

concepts.name: Alum mordant paste
concepts.description: Alum dissolved in water and thickened with a natural gum to a printable paste.

concepts.name: Printing the alum paste
concepts.description: The alum paste is printed with a carved wooden block wherever red is wanted.

concepts.name: Dyeing in a madder-type (hydroxyanthraquinone) bath
concepts.description: The printed cloth is simmered in a bath of madder-type dye — traditionally Rubia roots or Morinda, today often synthetic alizarin — whose colourants are hydroxyanthraquinones.

concepts.name: Red develops only where alum was printed
concepts.description: After dyeing, the alum-printed areas are red, while unprinted areas take only a weak stain.

concepts.name: Aluminium–hydroxyanthraquinone complex (lake) formation
concepts.description: The dye's adjacent hydroxyl and carbonyl groups chelate aluminium ions held on the fibre, forming an insoluble coloured metal complex (lake).

concepts.name: Wash-fast red print
concepts.description: The insoluble complex resists washing, giving a durable red.

concepts.name: Scrap iron fermented with jaggery
concepts.description: Scrap iron is left to ferment with jaggery (or molasses) and water for days to weeks, giving an iron-rich liquor.

concepts.name: Iron liquor (kat / syahi)
concepts.description: A solution of iron(II) salts of the organic acids formed during fermentation, thickened for printing.

concepts.name: Printing the iron liquor
concepts.description: The iron liquor is printed with outline blocks on the harda-treated cloth.

concepts.name: Black appears at once
concepts.description: The printed lines turn grey-black almost immediately, before any dye bath.

concepts.name: Iron–tannin (tannate) complex
concepts.description: Iron ions react with the tannin phenolic groups on the fibre, forming dark iron–tannate complexes, the same chemistry as iron-gall ink.

concepts.name: Black outlines of the design
concepts.description: Iron-tannin black gives the outlines and black grounds of the print.

concepts.name: Gradual weakening of iron-blacked areas
concepts.description: Iron-blacked areas of old textiles are often weaker or lost first, attributed to iron-catalysed degradation of cellulose.

concepts.name: Purple-brown to black where iron was printed
concepts.description: In the same madder-type bath, iron-printed areas turn purple, brown or near-black instead of red.

concepts.name: Iron–hydroxyanthraquinone complex
concepts.description: The same dye chelates iron instead of aluminium; the different metal complex absorbs light differently, giving a different hue.

concepts.name: Several colours from one dye bath
concepts.description: Printing different mordants lets a single dye bath produce reds, purples, browns and blacks in one operation.

concepts.name: Weak stain on unmordanted ground
concepts.description: Areas with no printed mordant pick up a pale, loosely held stain.

concepts.name: Thorough washing after dyeing
concepts.description: The dyed cloth is washed repeatedly in running water.

concepts.name: Removal of dye not held by a metal complex
concepts.description: Dye merely adsorbed on unmordanted cellulose is weakly held and washes out, whereas complexed dye stays.

concepts.name: Clean ground and sharp colour contrast
concepts.description: The background clears toward the pale harda tint, sharpening the contrast of the printed pattern.

concepts.name: Indigo
concepts.description: Indigo, the blue colourant from Indigofera leaves, supplied as a solid.

concepts.name: Indigo is insoluble in water
concepts.description: Indigo does not dissolve in water and cannot dye fibres as it is.

concepts.name: Setting an alkaline reducing vat
concepts.description: Indigo is reduced in an alkaline vat — traditionally by fermentation, with lime — to make it soluble.

concepts.name: Vat liquor is yellow-green with a coppery film
concepts.description: A working vat is yellowish-green, often with a coppery surface film, not blue.

concepts.name: Soluble leuco-indigo penetrates the fibre
concepts.description: Reduced (leuco) indigo is water-soluble and diffuses into the cotton fibres while the cloth is immersed.

concepts.name: Blue develops on exposure to air
concepts.description: Lifted from the vat the cloth turns from green to blue as air oxidises leuco-indigo back to insoluble indigo inside the fibre.

concepts.name: Fast blue built up by repeated dips
concepts.description: Insoluble indigo trapped in the fibre is wash-fast; repeated dip-and-air cycles deepen the shade.

concepts.name: Dabu mud-resist paste
concepts.description: A resist paste of fine clay, lime, natural gum and wheat chaff, aged and kneaded to a sticky consistency.

concepts.name: Printing the mud resist
concepts.description: The mud paste is block-printed on areas that must stay undyed.

concepts.name: Dusting with sawdust or fine dung
concepts.description: Sawdust or fine powdered dung is sprinkled on the wet paste.

concepts.name: Dried resist crazes with fine cracks
concepts.description: The dusted paste dries to a firm crust that develops fine cracks as the cloth is handled.

concepts.name: Paste physically blocks dye penetration
concepts.description: The dried clay crust physically seals the fibres so dye liquor cannot reach them; dye seeps only through the cracks.

concepts.name: Undyed pattern with fine veining
concepts.description: After dyeing and washing off the mud, the resisted pattern shows pale with a fine network of coloured veins.

concepts.name: Historical origin of dabu resist printing
concepts.description: When and where mud-resist block printing began in Rajasthan is not established by securely dated evidence.

concepts.name: Dye source of a particular historical print
concepts.description: Which plant (a Rubia species, Morinda, or another source) coloured a specific historical red cannot be inferred by eye; it requires chemical analysis of the colourants.

concepts.name: Natural gum thickener
concepts.description: Plant gums (e.g. acacia gum) are dissolved into mordant and iron pastes.

concepts.name: Raised paste viscosity
concepts.description: Dissolved gum makes the paste viscous and sticky rather than watery.

concepts.name: Block impression
concepts.description: The printer charges the carved block from a pad and strikes it firmly onto the cloth.

concepts.name: Crisp printed edges
concepts.description: Impressions from a well-thickened paste have crisp edges without haloes.

concepts.name: Limited capillary spreading
concepts.description: High viscosity slows capillary wicking of liquid along yarns, so the paste stays where it is placed.

concepts.name: Fine, well-defined print
concepts.description: Controlled spreading preserves fine lines and registration of the design.

concepts.name: Prepared clay body
concepts.description: Local clay cleaned of stones and roots, sometimes blended, ready to be worked.

concepts.name: Very fine, platy clay-mineral particles
concepts.description: Clay minerals occur as extremely small, flat, sheet-like particles with large surface area.

concepts.name: Kneading with water (wedging)
concepts.description: Water is worked into the clay and the mass is kneaded until uniform.

concepts.name: Deforms under pressure and holds its shape
concepts.description: The clay yields smoothly under the hands or on the wheel without cracking and keeps the new shape when released.

concepts.name: Water films between particles
concepts.description: Thin water films around the platy particles let them slide past one another while cohesive forces keep them together.

concepts.name: Plastic, formable clay body
concepts.description: The body can be thrown, coiled or moulded into vessels.

concepts.name: Freshly formed ware
concepts.description: Vessels just formed, still containing their water of plasticity.

concepts.name: Water of plasticity
concepts.description: The water added to make the clay plastic occupies the spaces between particles.

concepts.name: Drying the ware
concepts.description: The ware is dried, ideally slowly and evenly in shade, before firing.

concepts.name: Ware shrinks, and may warp
concepts.description: Vessels become visibly smaller and can distort if one side dries faster.

concepts.name: Particles draw together as inter-particle water leaves
concepts.description: As water between particles evaporates, particles move closer until they touch; shrinkage then largely stops.

concepts.name: Cracks where drying is uneven
concepts.description: Differential drying makes some parts shrink before others; the resulting stresses cause warping or cracking, especially at rims, handles and joins.

concepts.name: Temper (sand, grog or organic matter)
concepts.description: Non-plastic materials such as sand, crushed fired pottery (grog) or chopped plant matter added to the clay.

concepts.name: Coarse and non-plastic
concepts.description: Temper particles are coarse and do not shrink with the clay.

concepts.name: Mixing temper into the clay
concepts.description: The potter kneads a proportion of temper into the clay body.

concepts.name: Less shrinkage and a more open body
concepts.description: Tempered bodies shrink less and are more open-textured.

concepts.name: Pores for water escape and a rigid skeleton
concepts.description: Coarse grains form a rigid skeleton that restrains shrinkage and leaves pore paths through which water vapour escapes, while grain boundaries can stop cracks from spreading.

concepts.name: Fewer cracks and better thermal-shock resistance
concepts.description: Tempered ware cracks less in drying and firing, and cooking pots tolerate heating and cooling better.

concepts.name: Ware still slightly damp when set for firing
concepts.description: Ware appearing dry still holds some residual moisture.

concepts.name: Heating quickly at the start of firing
concepts.description: The fire is brought up fast from the start.

concepts.name: Spalling or bursting of pots
concepts.description: Flakes blow off surfaces or whole pots burst early in the firing.

concepts.name: Steam pressure in the pores
concepts.description: Water turning to steam faster than it can escape through the pores builds pressure.

concepts.name: Slow initial 'water-smoking' stage
concepts.description: Potters warm the ware slowly at first, or pre-dry it near the fire, until the residual water has gone.

concepts.name: Clay containing kaolinite-group minerals
concepts.description: A clay whose minerals include kaolinite.

concepts.name: Chemically bound hydroxyl water in the crystal structure
concepts.description: Kaolinite's layered structure contains hydroxyl groups — 'chemically combined water' distinct from pore water.

concepts.name: Firing past about 450–600 °C
concepts.description: The firing reaches temperatures above roughly 450–600 °C.

concepts.name: Fired clay no longer softens in water
concepts.description: After such firing a sherd placed in water stays hard instead of slaking back to mud.

concepts.name: Dehydroxylation to metakaolin
concepts.description: Hydroxyls leave as water vapour and kaolinite's structure collapses irreversibly to disordered metakaolin, which cannot rehydrate into plastic clay.

concepts.name: Permanent ceramic body
concepts.description: The irreversible change marks the transition from dried clay to ceramic.

concepts.name: Quartz grains in the body
concepts.description: Most clays and sand tempers contain quartz.

concepts.name: Rapid heating or cooling around 573 °C
concepts.description: The temperature passes quickly through the region around 573 °C, on heating or especially on cooling.

concepts.name: Cracks appear, especially on cooling (dunting)
concepts.description: Sharp cracks open, often heard as pinging while the kiln cools.

concepts.name: Alpha–beta quartz inversion
concepts.description: At 573 °C quartz changes reversibly and suddenly between its alpha and beta forms with an abrupt volume change, straining the surrounding body.

concepts.name: Heat and cool slowly through 573 °C
concepts.description: Potters avoid sudden draughts and fast cooling in this range.

concepts.name: Organic matter in the clay
concepts.description: Clays and organic tempers contain plant and humic material.

concepts.name: Short firing or limited oxygen
concepts.description: Firing is brief or the fuel-rich fire is starved of air.

concepts.name: Dark core in the sherd cross-section
concepts.description: A broken sherd shows a grey-black core between lighter surfaces.

concepts.name: Incomplete burnout of carbon
concepts.description: Carbon burns out from the surfaces inward and needs oxygen and time; where either is lacking, carbon remains in the core.

concepts.name: Black coring
concepts.description: The retained carbon (and reduced iron) forms a black core, recording the firing conditions.

concepts.name: Iron-bearing clay
concepts.description: Most terracotta clays contain several percent iron compounds.

concepts.name: Iron oxides and hydroxides
concepts.description: The iron occurs as oxides and hydroxides dispersed through the clay.

concepts.name: Controlling the firing atmosphere
concepts.description: The potter opens the fire to air, or smothers it with fuel, dung or sawdust to cut off oxygen.

concepts.name: Red-orange ware or grey-black ware
concepts.description: Air-rich firings give red-orange ware; smothered firings give grey to black ware.

concepts.name: Oxidation state of iron
concepts.description: In oxidising conditions iron forms red hematite (Fe2O3); in reducing conditions lower oxides such as magnetite or FeO form, grey to black.

concepts.name: Deliberate control of ware colour
concepts.description: Potters choose red or black ware by managing the atmosphere, especially at the end of firing.

concepts.name: Low-fired terracotta vessel
concepts.description: A water pot fired at low temperature without glaze.

concepts.name: Open, interconnected porosity
concepts.description: Low firing leaves the body porous with connected pores.

concepts.name: Filling the pot with water
concepts.description: The vessel is filled and kept in a shaded, airy place.

concepts.name: Outer surface feels damp and cool
concepts.description: The outside of a filled pot stays slightly damp.

concepts.name: Evaporation absorbs latent heat
concepts.description: Water seeping through the pores evaporates from the outer surface, absorbing latent heat and cooling the pot and its contents.

concepts.name: Water cooler than ambient air
concepts.description: Stored water stays noticeably cooler than the surroundings, most so in dry, breezy weather.

concepts.name: Leather-hard surface
concepts.description: Partly dried ware, firm but still slightly damp.

concepts.name: Burnishing with a smooth stone
concepts.description: The potter rubs the leather-hard surface with a smooth pebble or bone.

concepts.name: Glossy, lustrous surface
concepts.description: The rubbed surface takes on a sheen that survives low firing.

concepts.name: Alignment of platy particles at the surface
concepts.description: Pressure and rubbing align fine platy particles parallel to the surface and compact it, making it smooth and reflective.

concepts.name: Smoother, less permeable surface
concepts.description: The compacted surface is less permeable and more decorative.

concepts.name: Earliest use of a tempering practice in a region
concepts.description: When and where a particular tempering recipe was first used in a region is not established without dated archaeological and analytical evidence.

concepts.name: Carving blank
concepts.description: A block of seasoned timber selected and roughed out for carving.

concepts.name: Longitudinally aligned fibres (grain)
concepts.description: Most wood cells are long, hollow fibres aligned along the stem; grain direction in a blank often runs at a slope to its surfaces and changes around knots and curved figure.

concepts.name: Cutting against the grain
concepts.description: The gouge is driven so that its edge meets fibres rising toward it ('uphill').

concepts.name: Torn, rough surface (tear-out)
concepts.description: Fibres lift and tear below the intended surface, leaving pits and fuzz.

concepts.name: Wedge splits wood ahead of the edge
concepts.description: The tool acts as a wedge; when fibres slope up into the cut, the easy cleavage along the grain runs ahead of and below the edge, levering fibres out instead of severing them.

concepts.name: Detail lost; extra finishing needed
concepts.description: Tear-out below the surface destroys fine detail and must be removed by re-cutting from the other direction or by scraping.

concepts.name: Cutting with the grain
concepts.description: The edge is driven 'downhill', so the fibres slope away from the cut.

concepts.name: Clean, burnished cut surface
concepts.description: The cut leaves a smooth, often shiny surface.

concepts.name: Fibres severed while supported by wood beneath
concepts.description: Any splitting tends to run up and out of the work, so the edge severs fibres that are still supported below it.

concepts.name: Crisp fine detail
concepts.description: Clean severing preserves sharp ridges and fine undercuts.

concepts.name: Green (freshly cut) wood
concepts.description: Wood from a recently felled tree, with its cell walls saturated and cavities holding free water.

concepts.name: Moisture above the fibre saturation point
concepts.description: Green wood holds moisture above the fibre saturation point (on average about 30% moisture content), where cell walls are fully saturated.

concepts.name: Lower strength and hardness when green
concepts.description: Most strength properties, including hardness, are lower above the fibre saturation point and rise as wood dries below it.

concepts.name: Green wood carves easily
concepts.description: Carvers find green wood cuts with less effort and fewer broken edges.

concepts.name: Loss of bound water below the fibre saturation point
concepts.description: Drying first removes free water with no shrinkage; once moisture falls below the fibre saturation point, water leaves the cell walls and the walls shrink.

concepts.name: Anisotropic shrinkage
concepts.description: Shrinkage is largest tangentially (to the growth rings), roughly half that radially, and very small longitudinally.

concepts.name: Distortion and cracking of the carving
concepts.description: A carving finished green and then dried warps out of shape and may crack as different directions shrink by different amounts.

concepts.name: Round section containing the pith
concepts.description: A log or branch section carved in the round with the pith included.

concepts.name: Radial cracks opening from the pith
concepts.description: On drying, V-shaped cracks open radially from the pith outward.

concepts.name: Remove the pith or split the blank
concepts.description: Carvers avoid including the pith, split the blank through it, or dry the rough-out slowly before finishing.

concepts.name: Freshly felled logs and planks
concepts.description: Timber stacked to season after felling.

concepts.name: Rapid drying from end grain
concepts.description: Moisture moves along the grain many times faster than across it, so the ends of a piece dry much faster than its middle.

concepts.name: Tension in the drier shell
concepts.description: The drier region tries to shrink but is restrained by the wetter wood it is attached to, so it is put in tension.

concepts.name: End checks
concepts.description: Short cracks open on the end grain and run into the piece.

concepts.name: Sealing the end grain
concepts.description: The ends are coated with wax, paint or a proprietary sealer soon after cutting.

concepts.name: Less end checking
concepts.description: Slowing end drying reduces the stress gradient and the number and length of end checks.

concepts.name: Dense hardwood
concepts.description: A high-density species such as many rosewoods and other tropical hardwoods.

concepts.name: High density and hardness
concepts.description: Hardness and most strength properties increase with density (specific gravity).

concepts.name: Carving the dense species
concepts.description: The carver works the dense wood with the usual gouges and mallet.

concepts.name: Edges dull or chip quickly
concepts.description: Tools lose their keenness faster and fine edges may chip.

concepts.name: Higher cutting forces and abrasive wear on the edge
concepts.description: Denser wood requires higher cutting forces, stressing a thin edge; some species also contain silica or other mineral inclusions that abrade edges.

concepts.name: Stronger bevel and frequent honing
concepts.description: Carvers of dense woods hone more often and may use a slightly steeper, more robust bevel.

concepts.name: Finished carving in use
concepts.description: A completed carving kept indoors or outdoors.

concepts.name: Seasonal changes in relative humidity
concepts.description: The surrounding air's relative humidity rises and falls with the seasons and with heating or monsoon conditions.

concepts.name: Moisture content tracks equilibrium moisture content
concepts.description: Wood continually gains or loses moisture toward an equilibrium moisture content set by the air's relative humidity and temperature.

concepts.name: Seasonal swelling and shrinking
concepts.description: Joints open and close and panels move across the grain through the year.

concepts.name: Applying a surface finish
concepts.description: The carving is coated with oil, varnish, lacquer or wax.

concepts.name: Coatings slow but do not stop moisture exchange
concepts.description: Film-forming finishes resist water-vapour movement to differing degrees, but no practical coating stops it completely.

concepts.name: Movement reduced and slowed, not eliminated
concepts.description: A finished carving responds to humidity changes more slowly and less, damping short-term swings.

concepts.name: Linseed oil
concepts.description: Oil pressed from flax seed, used raw or heat-treated ('boiled').

concepts.name: Highly unsaturated fatty acids
concepts.description: Linseed oil is rich in polyunsaturated fatty-acid chains.

concepts.name: Rubbing oil into the carving
concepts.description: Thin coats are rubbed in, the excess wiped off, and left to cure between coats.

concepts.name: Surface darkens and gains a soft sheen
concepts.description: The wood darkens slightly and the figure becomes more pronounced.

concepts.name: Oxidative cross-linking (curing)
concepts.description: Oxygen from the air reacts with the unsaturated chains, cross-linking the oil into a solid polymer within and on the wood.

concepts.name: Penetrating, easily renewed finish with modest protection
concepts.description: The cured oil gives a natural-looking, easily repaired finish with modest water resistance.

concepts.name: Regional carving style
concepts.description: Regional traditions are distinguished by motifs, species and tooling habits.

concepts.name: Origin date of a regional carving style
concepts.description: The founding date, place or originator of a given regional carving tradition is generally not established by securely dated evidence; accounts are often oral and conflicting.
